speechtext: My right hon. friend must know that the three year branch line program was opposed in this house by Sir Henry Drayton, and that the Guysborough branch line was also opposed by him.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have just
alluded to the three year branch line proposal, and I said that proposal was defeated by the friends of my hon. friend in another house._ Those proposals were brought forward in the form of bills which were discussed here. I am now speaking of the proposals which came before the committee on railways and shipping, of which I think my hon. friend was a member and in the report of which at all events he acquiesced. So I say that so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, the legacy which was left hon. gentlemen opposite is one of which they, as well as those on this side of the house, might well speak with pride.
I wish now to go a step further and refer to the contention made by my right hon. friend that his predecessor in office should have anticipated the deficit at the end of the last fiscal year and should have levied more taxation. If my right hon. friend had that degree of foreknowledge which he says his predecessor in office should have possessed, how does he reconcile that knowledge and his hopes of attaining the position which he now holds with the promises he made throughout the campaign, that if returned to power he would, not by means of borrowing but by additional taxation, within a very short time construct a national highway, make grants with respect to unemployment, restore the grants with regard to technical education and agricultural instruction, give one hundred per cent of the
2676	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
cost of old age pensions to all the provinces, develop the St. Lawrence waterway, construct the Peace River outlet, build bridges in different parts of the country and see that they were exempt from tolls, build additional railways, and commit the country to a thousand and one other different kinds of public works? When my hon. friend says that last year anyone should have known what conditions would become, I ask him what he meant by telling the people of this country that if he were returned to power he would do all these things. To-day my right hon. friend is trying to make a reputation for himself as a gentleman who makes promises and also as a man of his word who keeps his promises.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And his following say "hear, hear", and cheer. May I say this to my right hon. friend, that if these various promises, only a fraction of which he is attempting to implement or will ever be able to implement, which mean so much in the way of taxation to the people of the country, were to involve anything in the way of sacrifice personal to himself, I would see some reason for the applause of his followers, but when the promises which were made so lightly for the purposes of winning an election can be implemented only out of the taxes of the people; when in addition they mean increased taxation at a time of great distress; when they mean that the burden which is already upon industry is to be increased; when they mean that the burden which is already upon every family and household of humble means and circumstances throughout this country is being increased, I fail to see where there is any very great credit coming to him. The promises of yesterday are the taxes of to-day.
My right hon. friend did not tell the electors that when he was appealing to them; he led them to believe there was some invisible source from which he. would be able to draw all that was needed in the way of revenue in order to provide for the things he was promising. If he had been honest with the electorate he would have said, " While I promise this to you, you must be prepared for increased taxation of a very extensive nature, taxation that directly or indirectly must fall on every one of you." I did not follow my right hon. friend in the line of promises; I understood something of the responsibility which rests upon one who takes a position of leadership either of a party or of a government, as well as of what the public has a right to expect of him.

May I say again to my right hon. friend what I said the other evening in his absence:
I believe that to-day the people of this country would be much more ready to forgive him a little delay in attempting to implement at their expense some of his innumerable promises than they will be ready to commend him for carrying out promises which for many years to come will weigh them down with additional burdens of taxation, I say to my right hon. friend that I think he ought to consider that aspect of the question very carefully; before he continues in the direction of recklessly spending public moneys, in which he appears to have started, he should give consideration to what this is going to mean, this inevitable sequel of vast taxation at this time of great distress.
Now may I refer to another statement my hon. friend has made, and which his friends are continually quoting. It is this, that the policies of the Liberal administration were responsible for the conditions which now exist. In answer to that statement may I make clear to my right hon. friend and to the country what must everywhere be known, namely that the Liberal policies which were framed [DOT] deliberately and definitely for the purpose of meeting the situation which exists to-day were defeated and destroyed at the instance of my right hon. friend and those who sit around him. The Liberal policies designed to cope with the depression were never given a chance. The Dunning budget was framed with regard to the conditions existing in Canada at the time, conditions which the then administration saw would continue for some time. That budget was framed with the intention of helping to further trade between this country and Great Britain and other countries; it was planned to expand the trade of Canada. It was framed with reference to an Imperial conference which was to take place in London in the fall of the year, and it was designed deliberately to meet a trying and difficult situation throughout the country. No sooner was it introduced than my right hon. friend led the way in denouncing it, in misrepresenting it, in decrying it, in ridiculing it and in doing all that he could to defeat it. Between his representations with respect to the Dunning budget, not only in this house, but on platforms from one end of the country to the other, and the promises he made, he defeated the very policies that would have helped to put Canada in a very different position from the one she is in to-day.
So I say, Mr. Speaker, that there is very little reason why my right hon. friend should say the policies of the Liberal party are in

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
any way responsible for the deplorable conditions of the present. May I ask him this: Was the Liberal party responsible for the fiasco which he made of the Imperial conference? I think he recognizes, as the world now recognizes, that that conference was a most dismal failure, that in every particular it left relations, not more pleasant and agreeable as between this country and the mother country, but rather distinctly unpleasant and disagreeable. The Liberal party cannot be blamed for that. Yet, as is known, the policies cif the Liberal party, with respect to trade with Great Britain, at the time they were enunciated in the house, caused men and women of all political parties in the mother country to enthuse at the prospect of the Imperial conference, and what it would mean to the different parts of the empire, and in particular to trade between Great Britain and Canada.
But not only did my right hon. friend before gaining power do what he could-and in which he was successful-to nullify the Liberal policies and prevent their being put into effect, but since assuming office he has brought in policies of his own which are diametrically the reverse of those advocated by the Liberal party. My right hon. friend called a special session of parliament, ostensibly for the purpose of dealing with unemployment; but in reality, as events proved, to alter the tariff of the country along high protectionist lines, restricting trade where the Liberal administration of the day had sought by the removal of restrictions to create further trade. Does he forget that by the very policies which he introduced at the special session of parliament he made trade more difficult, intensified the stagnation of trade, and made conditions worse than they were?
I say, therefore, that both with respect to the policies which he has introduced, and with respect to the policies of the Liberal party which he helped to destroy, my right hon. friend must assume responsibility for unemployment having become worse in this country instead of improving. He must shoulder also responsibility for the fact that the rural elements are finding it more difficult than otherwise would have been the case to secure markets.
May I point out what in my opinion the country believes to be the most serious aspect of what my right hon. friend has done and is doing. Time and again, in reference to the right hon. gentleman while pointing to what I believe to be his sincerity, and his faith in the objects he has in view, I have had to take
very strong exception to his judgment, and to his method of doing the things he attempts to do. I wish now to take very strong exception to the method my right hon. friend has adopted in dealing with the tariff of this country and to his judgment in matters of the kind.
He is not the first Minister of Finance who has had to do with tariff revision. We have almost the entire history of the country behind us to guide us in an understanding of what the leading men of Canada have regarded as the methods which should be adopted in matters of tariff revision. I say that there is nothing in the whole history of the Canadian tariff which will bear anything in the nature of a remote comparison or resemblance to what my right hon. friend has already done, and to the way in which he is proceeding.
From the days of Sir John Macdonald to the present moment, no Prime Minister, no government has thought fit to alter the tariff of the country in the way in which my right hon. friend has changed it; for he has made wholesale revisions in the tariff, reckless and ruthless in the extreme, raising the schedule to any point or on any item. Just so long as he is presented with some petition to put the tariff higher on any item, up it goes, still higher, until to-day we have a tariff which I venture to say even he himself could not describe to the people-a tariff beyond all description, so far as its height and general characteristics are concerned.
Let me review for a few moments the history of our tariff. Take the government of Sir John Macdonald. Look at the rates-of duties imposed by Sir John when he introduced the national policy and compare those rates with the duties enacted at the last special session and proposed at this session of parliament. Why, beside these- the rates imposed by Sir John Macdonald dwarf into insignificance. Yet I venture to say that Sir John Macdonald was as much concerned with the well-being of the manufacturers as is my right hon. friend. But Sir John had had an experience of many years which caused him, in matters that affected the whole financial, industrial and commercial structure of the country, to move with a good deal of caution. My right hon. friend apparently does not know the meaning of the word caution. His method of dealing with the tariff I have heard described as that of a running jump, a leap in the dark-any change so long as it is a change in the upward direction. Go through the revisions of the tariff made while Sir John Macdonald was in power, while Sir John Abbott was in power, or Sir John
3678	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
Thompson, or Sir Mackenzie Bowell, or Sir Charles Tupper, any of the sirs who made up the quintette of Conservative prime ministers of that day, and you will not find in regard to the administration of any one of them any changes comparable to those which my right bon. friend has brought about.
Let us come to the time when Sir Wilfrid Laurier took office. True, the Liberal policy with respect to the tariff was one which tended in a direction opposite to that of his predecessors in office and to that of my right hon. friend's policy. The changes made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier tended in the direction of reduced rather than of increased duties. But did the Liberal party when in office take hold of ithe tariff schedule and blue pencil tlhe whole of it, altering the levels and fixing purely arbitrary rates? Did the Liberal party make its reductions by wholesale altering of the rates by SO, 60, 90. 100 per cent? Yet, in the other direction, this and much more is what hon. gentlemen- opposite have done; adopting throughout an entirely arbitrary method. The Right Hon. Mr. Fielding was a very experienced Minister of Finance, of him I have heard my right hon. friend opposite speak in very high terms, as well he might; for every Canadian must respect the late Mr. Fielding's great capacity and ability as a Minister of Finance as well as his noble integrity. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite: How does the method adopted by Mr. Fielding with respect to tariff revisions compare with the method which my right hon. friend has followed and is following? Was there ever a minister of finance in Canada who enjoyed in greater measure the confidence of the entire manufacturing clas3 as well as of other sections of the community? Mr. Fielding, with his great experience, was exceedingly cautious. When introducing tariff changes he was always careful to stress the delicate relationship that existed between the tariff structures as a whole and the business and commerce and finance of the country. But my right hon. friend disregards altogether an example of that kind. In fact, he ignores it wholly: one might almost say that by the course he is adopting he seeks to ridicule it.
Coming to a later day, let us take the government of Sir Robert Borden, who came into office after a campaign which had been waged on the tariff as the, main issue. Sir Robert Borden made certain revisions in the tariff. He had as his Minister of Finance Sir Thomas White, who spoke for the government of Sir Robert Borden so far as tariff matters were concerned. Has my right hon. friend ever considered what method was adopted by these

gentlemen? Though he had a much longer experience in' public life than my right hon. friend, did Sir Robert Borden when in office go through the tariff schedule with a blue pencil, scoring out the old rates, making at random change after change, substituting always higher rates for those that then existed, and all without investigation? Look at the tariffs; they speak for themselves: the changes that were made were in most instances made with the greatest caution and care. Some were in an upward direction, while some tended downward; but they were made, as the government of that day believed, in some relation to the needs of the industry affected and as the result of careful examination.
Take the administration of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. Will anyone say that the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen was afraid to speak his mind or to take deliberate and far-reaching action if he thought it necessary so to do? And how did Mr. Meighen while Prime Minister deal with the tariff? He also campaigned the country on the necessity for a revision of the tariff upward, and he had as his Minister of Finance Sir Henry Drayton. When they were charged with the responsibilities of office those gentlemen were as careful as they could be in dealing with the great financial industrial and commercial structure of the country as it was affected by the tariff.
I wish now to put on the record one or two of the views expressed by conservative ministers. I give them to my right hon. friend because these gentlemen are members of his own party. This is the teaching on which the members of his party were brought up, and I believe that it is this teaching, rather than the example which my right lion, friend has set, that even to-day convinces them and more largely has their support. In -his budget speech of 1913 Sir Thomas White, the then Minister -of Finance, after touching upon the economic conditions of the day and drawing attention to the fact that there is always a delicate connection between business and a revision of tariffs, declared:
There is, I believe, a general consensus of opinion that anything in the nature of an extensive I'evision of the tariff is not called for by existing conditions and would be contrary to public interest.
That was Sir Thomas AVhite's opinion, that an excessive revision was contrary to the public interest. I do not know what Sir Thomas is thinking of the revision made by this budget; I should like to have a chance to talk in private with him concerning it.
In his budget speech of the following year, 1914, Sir Thomas White said:

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
The evils of a high protective tariff are too well known to make it necessary that I should discuss them here.
What is the nature of tariff being enacted by my right hon. friend? It is not a low protective tariff, it is not even a moderate protective tariff. A word which indicated greater heights than the word "high" would not begin to describe it; it is the highest possible tariff that either he or the country could conceive of. "The evils of a high protective tariff" are the words used Iby Sir Thomas White. Hon. gentlemen who have been advocating protection have, I think very wisely, been saying that it must be moderate protection, must be protection having some regard to the relations of this country with other countries, and the business of this country with other countries. The word "moderate" has no place in my right hon. friend's vocabulary. Remember that Sir Robert Borden was the leader of the party at the time at which Sir Thomas White was the Minister of Finance.
Now I come to Sir Henry Drayton and his views. Sir Henry Drayton was Minister of Finance in Mr. Meighen's administration. In 1920, outlining the principles which should govern any revision of the tariff, he said:
As a means of raising revenues the tariff should be so adjusted as to place the chief burden upon those best able to bear it. Articles of luxury should be heavily taxed through the imposition of customs and excise rates. Food commodities and other necessaries of life, not produced or manufactured in Canada, should, if taxed at all, bear only such imposts as are necessary for revenue purposes. Those produced in Canada should be subjected to such customs duties only as may be necessary in the general national interest to be determined after strict investigation from time to time.
And later Sir Henry continued as follows:
For the purpose of encouraging the fullest development of our natural resources the tariff should be so adjusted as to permit machinery and the implements of production to be purchased at prices that will compare equitably with those paid in other countries for similar articles.
The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, then Prime Minister, stated during the course of the budget debate of 1920 that we in Canada could not afford to have an immoderate or high tariff. I would suggest to hon. members on the opposite side of the house who come from the western provinces, and who are so lightly voting the tariff proposals of this budget into the statutes, that they listen to the words which Mr. Meighen used on that occasion. He said:
So I say we cannot have any immoderate or high tariff for the reason that it tends to exclude that healthy element of fair conditions,
namely foreign competition. Secondly, we have in Canada a territory of wide extent. We have a portion of Canada newer than the other portion-a more predominating agricultural country newer to manufactures and agricultural development and consequently the advantages of tariff do not accrue as yet.
Later he stated:
Upon account of these two reasons we must always have in this country nothing more than a moderate tariff under any conditions whatsoever.
Whether those conditions be depression or great prosperity, because the west is in a different position from the east. Mr. Meighen considered that "we must always have in this country nothing more than a moderate tariff under any conditions whatsoever." He continues :
That will be the purpose of the revision under the principles clearly set out and enumerated by the Minister of Finance to which we adhere.
That should help to convince hon. gentlemen opposite that it might be well to endeavour to persuade their leader that if he is going to be true with respect to the principles of protection which the party has championed in the past, he should return to the use of the word "moderate." or at least another term which would suggest some modicum of reason in the changes which he is making. The extremes to which he has gone and is going is one of the most serious aspects of the whole situation.
In contrast to the changes which have been made by the present administration and which are now being proposed, running, as I have said, up into the hundreds of per cent, let me enumerate some of the changes made by the Liberal party during the time it was recently in office. They were changes in an opposite direction, but they were effected only after the most careful examination. May I point out that it was under these changes that Canada reached the position of prosperity which she enjoyed just prior to the time the world depression affected *this country along with others. That is a point which I would like hon. members to consider carefully. We are dealing at the moment with the condition of the country in a state of depression, and are considering what is best for the country in order to get it out of that depression. We have before us certain changes which in the past were made, and which at a time of depression helped to bring about prosperity. With that example before them this government should be careful in proceeding too far in a direction diametrically opposite.
In 1922 reductions were made on sugar, agricultural implements, textiles, boots and
2680	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
shoes. In 1923 the tariff on goods imported under the British preferential tariff was reduced by 10 per cent wherever the regular rate of duty exceeded 15 per cent and where the goods were imported directly to a sea or river port in Canada. The duty was reduced on sugar.
These changes were made with a view to helping the country at a time of depression, and in order to make the cost of agricultural implements as cheap as possible, having regard to the effect of the tariff upon their price. At a time when the people were being hard pressed and finding it difficult to make ends meet, the rate oni articles consumed by the great body of the people, such as sugar and commodities of that kind, was reduced.
In 1924 the duty was reduced on instruments of production used in agriculture, mining, forestry and fisheries. That was an important and far-reaching revision. In 1925 there was a reduction on well-drilling machinery and engines used for fishermen's boats. In 1926 the duties on automobiles were reduced, also a most important revision. It led to an immediate and substantial reduction in prices to Canadian purchasers. The duties were reduced on sugar, tin plate and so forth. In 1928 further reductions were made on the implements of production in the mining and fishing industries, and fertilizers were placed on the free list. There was a revision of the textiles tariff to provide for a reduction of the maximum duty under the general tariff from 37^ per cent to 30 per cent, with but a single exception. In 1930 tea was made free under the British preference, thus effecting to the consumer a reduction in the price of tea of from ten to fifteen cents per pound. Porcelain and chinaware were made free of duty under the British preference, which preference was extended to many products of the iron and steel industry. Fresh vegetables and fruits were made free under the British preference which applied to Bermuda and the West Indies.
The changes made during the time the Liberal administration was in office were of a character to help to meet the needs of the situation, to help to meet the condition with which the country was faced. Speaking broadly, the Liberal party during the time it was in offiee helped to bring the country out of a slough of despond similar to what we have at the present time into a position of prosperity which continued up to the moment the present world depression began to affect this country. It is important briefly to review the more important steps taken to that end.

In the first place, the Liberal party sought to effect economies in public administration. When we came into office there were many public services that had grown up during the period of the war. These were no longer necessary and were gradually eliminated. As I have already said, public expenditures were kept well within current revenues. We did not borrow to meet any expenditures on capital account. We found when we came into office, just as hon. gentlemen opposite find to-day, that the choice lay between increased taxation or the discontinuance of certain obligations created by grants which, under the circumstances, we felt we would not be justified in renewing. I refer to the different grants in aid that had been instituted prior to our coming into office. There the Liberal party found itself encumbered in a way in which the present government does not find itself encumbered. There had been placed on the statute book prior to the time we came into office measures which required annual payments of large sums of money to the provinces in addition to the subsidies provided for by statute-I want that point to be kept in mind-in addition to the subsidies which were fixed by statute this country was committed to large annual payments on account of technical education, on account of agricultural instruction, on account of highways, on account of coordination of employment offices, loans for housing, and several other services that I might mention. On June 2, I placed before the house a statement of what these various grants in aid came to, and I think I was able to show that if they were brought together into a ten-year period they would mean a payment to the provinces of something like $50,000,000 over and above the sums to which the provinces were entitled by way of subsidies paid in the regular way. The subsidies only amounted to between two and three times the amount that as grants in aid the previous Conservative government had committed this parliament to pay in addition to aid provincial governments to carry out obligations which were primarily their own.
The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) who spoke this afternoon, could not refrain from making the same misrepresentation members of his party have been continuing to make about the use of the word "vicious" as applied to a certain system of financing. He sought to convey the impression that I was opposed to the federal government having to do with these various services. I have never spoken in opposition to the federal government undertaking for itself work which came within its own sphere

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
and carrying through that work under appropriations made by this parliament and over which this parliament could exercise control. I have not been opposed to old age pensions, I have not been opposed to highways, I have not been opposed to the payment of unemployment relief-I have not been opposed to technical education, agricultural instruction, or to any of these services. But I have been opposed to the principle of one administration raising the taxes and handing the money thus raised over to another government to spend and itself having no control over the expenditure of the money so raised. I have very good authority, I think, for the unwisdom of such a course of action.
It may have cost us something in a political way to seek to protect the treasury by not continuing these various measures as the time for their renewal expired. There were two reasons for not renewing them. One was that when they were passed by this parliament it was never intended that they were to become perpetual. They were granted for a term of years, and at the end of that term, after giving due notification, we allowed the various grants in aid to run out. The other was we did not think the federal treasury should be thus further burdened. To that extent we have saved my right hon. friend a tremendous load at the present time; he is not encumbered as we were by such commitments. His encumbrances to-day are not in the nature of anything that has been left to him by the Liberal party. They are encumbrances shared in part in common with ourselves from a previous Conservative administration which left the whole obligation of the war to be met by others by reason of its failure to raise any revenues for the purpose at the time and which issued the tax exempt bonds. He has been freed by our action from the encumbrance of continuous expenditure on the grants in aid to which I have referred. The real encumbrance he has is one which he has put around his own neck-the encumbrance of promises of all kinds which he made and which he is obliged to meet, to the extent that he meets them at all, by the imposition of more in the way of taxation. That is where my right hon. friend's dilemma is to-day. He is increasing taxation on every side, not because he believes in the wisdom of the course he is taking, but simply that it may not be said that he was not prepared to act regardless of the consequences. I am the last one to suggest that any promise should be broken, but, as I have already said, I think my right hon. friend could well afford to say to the people: Before I continue to reenact various statutes in the nature of grants in aid to the provinces, I will
call a Dominion-provincial conference; I will discuss with the provinces the whole question of the relation of the finances of the provinces and those of the dominion, and after we have gone over the ground together and considered what amounts should be paid from the federal treasury to the provinces, I will bring down to parliament the measures that may be agreed upon. I suggest that he consider adopting that course. I think he would be justified in saying before dealing further with promises, given for purely political reasons, that in view of the present depression, and the extent to which it is involving increased burdens of taxation upon industry and individuals, he intends to have a discussion with the provinces and settle what is a fair and just distribution of the burden between them and the dominion. He might then assume to the full the federal obligation which is his and ask them to assume to the full the provincial obligation which is theirs. That would effect economy, that would avoid extravagance.
Another reason wthich accounte for the position to which we were able to bring the country was that our policies so far as the tariff was concerned aimed directly at two things of first importance in the development of trade. One was the reduction of the costs of production, and the other a reduction in the cost of living. Look over the tariffs that were introduced, study the different items, and you will see that an effort was made to free the great primary industries of agriculture, lumbering, mining and fishing of some part of the burden which the customs tariffs of the day were placing upon them. We did that believing that only as production costs were lowered would it be possible for those engaged in the primary industries to hold their own in the markets of the world. That was the first step. As these primary industries increase and prosper, so will all the secondary industries increase and prosper as well. The trouble with my right hon. friend's legislation is this, that so far as the industrial pyramid is concerned, he is viewing it upside down. He is focusing all his thoughts upon the secondary industries. All his legislation relates primarily to special privilege for the manufacturing industries, whereas the degree of success dependent on manufactures must in this country at least depend in the long run upon the successful development of the great basic industries of agriculture, lumbering, mining and fishing. If my hon. friend's government would do what the Liberal administration did, seek to make production in these great primary industries more profitable, he would find the trade of the country expanding, he would find our products getting
3682	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
markets in all parts of the world, and he would find that in return there would flow back into
the pockets of those engaged in those industries what is needed in the way of purchasing power to supply a home market for the manufacturers. But he has gone the other way about it. His whole thought is focused on the secondary industries, and he is not doing at all what he should in the way of development of the primary industries.
Similarly with regard to the cost of living. This budget, when you consider it in relation to the tariff and taxation, means a vast increase in the cost of living to the people of this country, and as the cost of living increases in Canada it is going to have itscffect on the cost of manufactured articles as well. Those additional costs will be passed on to the products of the primary industries as well. Canada to-day, if she is to hold her own, must hold it in world markets as well as in the domestic market, but these increased costs will further handicap her. So I repeat this house might well afford, before it passes this budget, to consider the steps taken after careful study and investigation by the previous Liberal administration in helping to bring the country to the position of prosperity which it attained.
Again, there was under Liberal administration the removal of different barriers to trade, which are indicated in the tariff changes made and in the measures with relation to taxation to which I have referred. But there was another step equally important, and that was the care with which the administration of the day sought to make an equitable distribution of the burdens of taxation. When we found the condition of the country depressed, we sought to remove the taxes from those least able to bear them, and we sought to impose the burden of necessary taxes upon those best able to bear it. Look over the record of the Liberal administration and you will see that that is true. But my right hon. friend's policies in all these things have been in a diametrically opposite direction. He has reversed our policies. Take the matter of public expenditures. He had not been in office above a few hours before, without authority of parliament, he extended a contract on the Welland canal amounting to $2,000,000, as though this great capital expenditure would not have to be met by taxation a little later.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What was done was this: The Liberal government of the day asked parliament to vote an amount to spend on the Welland canal sufficient for that fiscal year. Parliament voted that amount, $7,000,000. Parliament, not the government, voted that amount, and I say that when parliament voted $7,000,000, and did not vote $9,000,000, the present administration had no right to allow the contractors to go on and get another $2,000,000. However, that is the way in which taxes are speedily increased-like the various grants in aid, which my right hon. friend is continuing.
May I say a further word or two with respect, to - grants in aid and other public expenditures for political reasons? My right hon. friend, when in opposition, expressed himself very freely and very fluently and very strongly with regard to the duties of the head of a government, and with regard to what should be done in order to protect the exchequer. He was very strong upon the necessity for having a sinking fund. Over and over again he said that it was a necessary precaution against the pressure that would come from political supporters. Well, no man has had more political pressure brought to bear on him than my right hon. friend has had in the short time he has been in office, but he has not introduced any sinking fund, although, to listen to his words, which I shall quote, one would have thought that he would have done so at the earliest opportunity. On March 13, 1928, the present Prime Minister spoke as follows :
I say that we should place upon the statute books of this country at the earliest possible moment-
That is not a year hence:
-a provision by which a sinking fund will be set up such as they have in Great Britain and in other countries, so that we shall be enabled, within a period to be mentioned, absolutely to wipe out and eliminate the national debt of Canada.

Criminal Code-Bail
What is the province of Ontario doing? Do hon. gentlemen realize that in Ontario they have provided for the setting aside, of $3,000,000 every year so that at the end of forty years their debt will be entirely wiped ont, half being provided by public utilities, and the other half from the taxpayers of the province itself? Do hon. gentlemen realize that?
Suppose we seek to retire only $1,500,000,000 of this debt by a statutory sinking fund, by means of a provision placed upon the statute books of this country, so that the demands and pressure by political supporters would not induce the finance minister to part with public moneys because he would have to meet these sinking fund payments. It would ensure economy in the public service, and what is more, it would make the people of this country increasingly proud as they saw what President Coolidge has described as this greatest menace to our economic development, this great load of debt hanging over our necks, being gradually retired. . .
Is this country to continue to be menaced by this economic evil, by this debt hanging over our heads? Are we to continue, of all countries in the world, to make no provision for the future? Are we to be content to expend our patrimony day by day, without putting anything aside to take care of the long days of the future that are before us? I say it is unfair to ourselves, it is unfair to the taxpayers of this country to extract from them each year these increasingly large sums of money and make no provision for the retirement of our national obligations. . .
It has been said that no government is ever defeated because it is extravagant. That well may be. It well may be that the people may be debauched with their own revenues, and be taught that all you have to do is to spend their taxes freely among them and then you have succeeded, but what is the effect upon the life of a nation as a nation?
Has my right hon. friend changed his point, of view since he came into office and had the responsibility of being Prime Minister? Has he given up thinking about the nation as a nation and what it is going to come to? Is he to-day seeking to debauch the people of this country by their own taxes for the sake of remaining in power, when only a short time ago, standing here in this house, he was full of virtue in his admonition of the government of the day? I ask my right hon. friend whether he thinks that sort of thing constitutes the consistency, of which he likes to speak so often as a jewel.
I do not know where my right hon. friend's colleague the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan). is at the moment, but he, too, held very decided view's in regard to this important matter of distributing public moneys to provinces for all kinds of purposes, and the effect it was likely to have upon the exchequer. Let me read what the present Secretary of State said in this house on April 15, 1926:
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in the recent political history of this country we have proceeded altogether too far in the way of cooperation between the federal government and the provincial governments in respect, for instance, to road appropriations, which are within the proper jurisdiction and control of local legislatures. The same refers also to certain build-ding schemes in which there was cooperation, but in respect of which the federal treasury, which provided the money, really had little or no control over the management of the funds and little or no supervision over the actual expenditures made. I do not want to stress the matter, but I went through for several weeks, as counsel, an investigation in my native province of Nova Scotia which clearly disclosed to me that when provincial governments or provincial legislatures are expending moneys which are not raised on their own credit and responsibility, and in respect to which their sole responsibility is that of expenditure, it leads to wasteful expenditure and very wide latitude indeed in the making of those expenditures.
May I say to my right hon. friend and his colleagues, who when in opposition gave to' the administration of the day the advice to which I hare referred, that I think at the present time they could not more fittingly carry out the wishes of the people of this country than themselves to take to heart and to follow out with some degree of consistency the policies with respect to economy and political behaviour which they were so fond of outlining during the time they were in opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT TRIAL COURT OR COURT OF APPEAL MAY ADMIT APPELLANT TO BAIL
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT TRIAL COURT OR COURT OF APPEAL MAY ADMIT APPELLANT TO BAIL
speechtext: Under the present section 1019, if a person is convicted and wishes to lodge an appeal against the conviction, he is obliged to go to the chief justice or the aicting chief justice in order to do so. This sometimes occasions considerable inconvenience and expense, because in the ease of country lawyers they must go to the provincial headquarters, where the chief justice resides, and prepare all their papers and notices and so on. This amendment simply entitles the trial judge, if an appeal is lodged in the proper way, to grant hail. As a matter of fact I have known of cases where- bail has been refused by the trial judge and the person has remained in jail for three months, after which the conviction was set aside, because sometimes the chief justice has very strong views as to whether bail should be granted at all. This is simply to enable the trial judge to grant bail, if, in his opinion, the case is one which should be reviewed by the appeal court.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT TRIAL COURT OR COURT OF APPEAL MAY ADMIT APPELLANT TO BAIL
speechtext: I wonder if the Minister of Justice would explain to the house what section of the ' criminal code is affected, and whether this will be applicable to the whole of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT TRIAL COURT OR COURT OF APPEAL MAY ADMIT APPELLANT TO BAIL
speechtext:
Yes, it is applicable to all Canada. This bill proposes to amend section 1019 of the criminal code, which provides that the chief justice, the acting chief justice or a member of the court of appeal designated by him, may, if he deems fit, on the application of an appellant, admit the appellant to bail pending the determination of his appeal. In practice I do not think any great inconvenience has resulted from the present section. The courts of appeal in the various provinces usually sit at a central point; all parties know how to reach that point. The means of communication are good in all parts of Canada now, so that no very great inconvenience arises from the fact that a man who has been convicted and who desires to appeal must apply for bail pending the hearing of his appeal either to the chief justice of the

court of appeal of the province, the acting chief justice in case of the illness or absence of the chief justice, or to any other judge ot the court of appeal designated for that purpose.
My hon. friend who has introduced this bill desires to give that power to the trial court or the court of appeal. The court of appeal is defined in our act, and I am inclined to think that the wording of the bill would involve application to the full court of appeal, which would make the matter more difficult than it is at present. "Court of appeal" as defined in the criminal code includes, in the province of Ontario, the appellate division of the Supreme Court of Ontario, which means the full court. And so in all the other provinces. I think the language of the proposed amendment is objectionable in that, respect and I would suggest that my hon. friend amend it. I believe his intention is that the application for bail may be made to the judge who has conducted the trial, the trial judge, or to a single judge of the court of appeal. I do not see any very great objection to the principle of this bill. It seems to me that the trial judge, who is seized of all the facts, having heard the evidence, would be a very fit judge before whom an application for bail should be made. I agree that any judge of the court of' appeal would be a proper judge to whom such an application might be made. I do not see any objection in principle to the amendment, though I believe it might involve some little inconvenience; but I think the language should be changed. Instead of the words "triaj court" there should be substituted the words "trial judge." But I think it should be a judge of a superior court of the province, and not a judge of the district or county court. At present application must be made to a judge of the court of appeal who is either the chief justice or acting chief justice. We should provide that application should be made to the trial judge, if a judge of the superior court of the province, or to a judge of the court of appeal in the province. If an amendment were made to that effect there would be no objection to the bill.

subtopic: FORGING OF TRADE MARKS-SALE OF GOODS FALSELY MARKED

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, May 15, consideration in committee of Bill No. 34, to amend the criminal code (trade marks)- Mr. Geary-Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 1-Forgery.

subtopic: FORGING OF TRADE MARKS-SALE OF GOODS FALSELY MARKED
speechtext:
The last time the bill was before the house the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary), who has charge of it, omitted to make the customary explanation on the second reading, and in committee he was allowed by the chairman to make a few remarks regarding the general principle of this legislation under the section which we are now discussing. Under the same privilege
I was allowed to reply to him, and I trust that privilege will be extended to me now to .continue my remarks. As a matter of fact, it does not make a great deal of difference, because there are only three sections in the bill and they are all so interlocked that one could not very well discuss any one section without discussing the principle of the bill, and vice versa,
I see two objections to the bill but first I would point out, if I might presume to do so, being a layman, that it is what I would call rather sloppy legislation. The explanatory note reads:
The object of this bill is to cover omissions in the present wording of the relative sections in the criminal code relating generally to forgery of trade marks, labels, etc.
Where, how and when anyone could forge a label I should like to know. You might as well charge a man with forging a chair or a horse. You can forge something printed on a label but you cannot forge a label; you might as well speak of forging an envelope. The whole tenor of the bill is based on the mistaken idea that you can regard a label as a trade mark, and speak of the forging of a label, constituting a criminal offence in that respect, I shall deal with that point later on. At the moment I would point out to the Minister of Justice the initial difficulty with which we are faced when we speak of forging a label. I have never heard of foiging a label, but a trade mark can be forged.
The principle underlying this bill-and I would ask the house whether it is in the best interests of Canada to recognize that principle in legislation-is one of encouraging crime. It encourages, stabilizes, regulates and thereby admits the practice of what is commonly known as bootlegging. It is a principle which is denounced by all authorities on parliamentary law. Many years ago in England the Contagious Diseases (Human) Act was repealed for this very reason, that it condoned, encouraged, legalized or at any rate recognized vice. In adopting this principle we are putting bootlegging almost on the level of an occupation. It is an occupation which should be regarded as disreputable and one that should not be recognized by law. It is very obvious that that is the idea because I referred to that when the hon. member for South Toronto was introducing the bill. At that time the hon. member stated that the bill was introduced at the request of certain persons who were interested, and then later on he said:
At least it is creating difficulties among the consumers of certain of the manufactures of those industries.

Criminal Code-Trade Marks
I then asked the hon. member what those industries were, and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) interjected the word "spirits." Perhaps that remark was made in a spirit of humour, but the hon. member for South Toronto continued:
[DOT]-commodities in the production of which Canada I understand stands second to none, are sometimes deceived by reproductions of the product being forged upon them at the price of the original and proper product. We do not want that to occur, because it would seem to be a dangerous practice.
I assume the hon. member was referring to the customers. At that time I had made only a casual inspection of the bill and I did not understand the meaning of it until I read the hon. member's statement in Hansard. Since then I have had further enlightenment as to the purport of the bill through seeing the following statement in one of the Toronto papers, I believe the Mail and Empire. This article first comments upon the fact that the hon. member for South Toronto had introduced the bill, and then it says:
Probably a good deal of liquor is peddled under forged labels,-
There is the mistaken idea that you can forge a label. The article continues:
-and the dominion and provincial governments suffer loss. But the greatest victim of the practice is the unwary customer who takes it for granted that an official-looking label guarantees the purity of the contents of the bottle.
The hon. member who introduced the bill has stated that it is necessary-in whose interests? In the interests of the consumers of the contents of the bottles, whatever they may or may not contain. It may be said that that statement conflicts with my previous statement that we were encouraging, legalizing, regulating and thereby giving a legal status to bootleggers, whereas this bill deals with the customers of bootleggers. That is one end of the question, but I was talking about the other end. In these cases there are always two criminals involved, and we are asked to look lightly at the one and severely at the other, but the criminality or the responsibility rests as much on the one as on the other. If it were not for the customers there would be no bootlegging, and when we take steps to protect the customers of the bootleggers are we not putting the bootlegger himself on a legal basis and giving a sort of qualified assent to his engaging in the business? I do not know but that on some occasions the customer is the more guilty and more reprehensible of the two. Which is the worse, a young profligate who frequents a house of ill-fame or the wretched inmate who has been 
driven by extreme want to engage in that business? If I had to defend one or the other, not perhaps at the bar of conventional morality but at the bar of divine justice, I think I would rather take the case of the inmate than that of the customer. I shall not press the analogy too closely in this case, but still it remains. One does not need to go to the bootlegger unless he wants to, and if everyone keeps away from the bootlegger then this bill would not be necessary.
At this point I want to raise a point of order, not based on the rules of the house, under which I have been somewhat weirdly unfortunate of late, but rather on the common sense and fairness which is in the mind of every hon. member trying to legislate for the common good of Canada. I ask this committee:	Does it think it is good legislation
to pass this bill under the circumstances? Last year this house legislating on behalf of Canada cut this country off from a revenue of something like $20,000,000 by prohibiting or refusing clearances to those people who were shipping bootleg liquor over to the United States. Why did we do it? Was there any money in it for us? Not at all, we lost $20,000,000. Were we compelled by any legal compulsion under the terms of a treaty with a friendly nation? Not at all, we were instigated solely by the idea that it was the decent thing to do, that we should not be made the vehicle for illegal transactions or the breaking of the laws of a friendly nation which, whether rightly or wrongly, had adopted the principle of prohibition. This country was being made the jumping-off ground for the breaking of that law, and we took a big, wide viewpoint and said: We will not be a party to it, even though it costs us a lot of money.
If this bill is passed, its provisions will apply to all of Canada. If it were restricted to Toronto alone I might have less objection to it-let that city work out its own solution of its own troubles. The legislation to which I referred was passed last year, and every member of the committee knows what happened this year. An hon. member opposite introduced a resolution aimed at the repealing of that section of the law, and the committee knows how it was received. It was not necessary to take a vote, and if a vote had been taken there would probably have been only one vote recorded in favour of the resolution, whereas last year eleven hon. members stood up and voted against the bill being passed at that time. Public sentiment has crystallized and has informed itself, and the other day the house was practically unanimous in favour of continuing this legis-

Criminal Code-Trade Marks
lation. If this bill is passed, in what position do we place ourselves? We will be reversing our policy and going back to encourage this practice. The very minute you begin to regulate a practice you acknowledge its existence and give it a sort of status quo. We would be encouraging a practice in connection with which we already have taken a very definite step to forbid.
There have been cases in the past where a law has become obsolete or by long nonusage has been allowed gradually to fall into disuse. Under such circumstances there might be a need for legislation such as this, but that is not the present case. The province of Ontario, like many of the other provinces, has in its good judgment passed a law under which its citizens can buy liquor and beer of any description in practically unlimited quantities. This liquor is sold at government stores under very careful regulations; the quality is guaranteed and the price is regulated, presumedly on a satisfactory basis or else there would not be so much of it sold. The hours during which these stores remain open have been fixed by the representatives of the people at Toronto and apparently are satisfactory to the residents of that province. I have before me a press despatch dated Toronto, May 9, headed "Ontario's Liquor Profits More Than $9,000,000." This article reads as follows:
Revenue from the sale of liquor and liquor permits,-
I must admit this figure includes the permits.
-gave the Ontario provincial government a total profit of $9,315,967.30 last year, according to the Ontario Liquor Control Board's annual report.
The article contains other data which I need not read. The committee knows that a very comfortable profit was made. I think it would be safe to assume that if the net profit was $9,000,000, the gross tum-over probably would be $40,000,000, and that in one comparatively-well, I will not call it a small province, but at all events in one province of Canada. Multiply it by nine and you get some idea of the liquor that is bought and sold in these hard times throughout the dominion. This is Ontario alone that consumes $40,000,000 worth, and all of it- because it is recorded in that way by the liquor board-is sold legally under government auspices. That leaves out possibly the large amount that goes through the bootleggers' hands, with which this bill concerns itself.
Now this is the situation. These people who consume $40,000,000 worth are not satisfied; they must go out and patronize bootleggers, because certainly if there were no demand for illicit liquor there would be no bootlegging. Then when they get stung, to use the common expression, they squeal about it and come to us for protection. Even men whose liquor is hi-jacked know better than to do that; they take their medicine and say nothing. I recall a good many years ago going with a party of young men who went for what we now call bootleg stuff. We went down a back lane, a dark alley, clambered over some loose boards and finally reached an iron-clad door.

subtopic: FORGING OF TRADE MARKS-SALE OF GOODS FALSELY MARKED
speechtext: You had a wonderful experience.

subtopic: FORGING OF TRADE MARKS-SALE OF GOODS FALSELY MARKED
speechtext:
I am only using it as an
illustration, but possibly it has awakened in the hon. gentleman some memories of when ho too was young and innocent. I was describing this mythical Bill Jones' career-if I may put it in that way. He came to this iron-clad door-he discovered afterwards why it was so protected-in which he found a little shutter He gave a certain knock, the shutter was opened, he shoved in $5 and received a bottle with a whispered injunction not to open it until he got out of town because the place was being watched. After getting into a thirty below zero atmosphere some distance out of town he opened his bottle and found that it was tea-very good tea, but a little dear at $5 a bottle. Naturally his first impulse was to go back and tear the house down, but after a while he laughed and acknowledged that he had been stung. Did he go to the legislature for redress? Not a bit of it. I believe on one occasion a man-he was probably a thrifty soul-went to the chief of police and complained. The chief asked him, "Were you buying tea?" The man said: "No." "Well, what were you buying?" "I was buying liquor." "Well, get out of here. You had no business buying liquor." That is all the sympathy he got. He never came to the legislature and complained that when he shoved $5 through the wicket he got tea instead of whiskey.
I remember seeing a small boy run to his mother and complain that his little comrade Bill Smith had hit him on the nose. Rather to my surprise the mother did not at once take his part; she probably knew her offspring better than I did. She said, "What were you doing to Bill Smith before he hit you on the nose?" This and a few other questions elicited the fact that he had thrown a stone at his little comrade and had nearly torn his ear off. So the mother very wisely

Criminal Code-Trade Marks
impressed on her offspring the moral: Leave crime alone, and you will not get into trouble. I think the illustration is a very appropriate and timely one.
If we pass this bill we will place ourselves in the horrible position of compounding a felony. I ask you again, sir, is it to stop bootlegging? If that were its purpose I would be for the bill with both hands. But it is not: its purpose is to protect the customer Tighten the law against bootlegging, if you like, but, as I shall show, there is no genuine attempt to do so here. The purpose of the bill is to protect whom? The person who goes to an illegal place for an illegal purpose. That person deserves no sympathy if he does not get what he expected. Will hon. members kindly listen to this quotation from the Mail and Empire?
The greatest victim of the practice is the unwary consumer who takes it for granted that an official-looking label guarantees the purity of the contents of the bottle.
So evidently it is the customer whom it is sought to protect.
Out in British Columbia we have a worse condition of affairs. There the danger is not so much the buying of bootleg liquor as the selling of narcotics which are far deadlier than liquor. The trouble there is to secure convictions, because of course, the man who buys narcotics is equally guilty with the peddler and on conviction can be given a jail sentence. But the law looks on the addict in a different light from the way in which it regards the bootlegger, for the addict is a man of weak will. The man or woman who falls a prey to narcotics has practically no will power left at all, and it has been proved that an addict will commit murder under the impulse to satisfy the craving for drugs. Consequently the law does not treat the addict so severely as the man who peddles narcotics. Then of course these wretched people who are ready to do anything to obtain their supply often get very inferior stuff. This is common knowledge. At the very best they will get a cheap grade although they pay a price appropriate for heroin which I think is the highest grade of that particular stuff. Suppose someone from Vancouver were to bring in a bill providing that when one of these wretched men went to a peddler he should be guaranteed the quality of the drug he was buying? That might be fair, but it would not appeal to the good sense of the house. That is because the purpose of our law is to prevent the illegal sale of narcotics as well as of liquor, which is the principle on which the whole system hinges.

There is a theory of law, I understand, which is expressed somewhat in this way, that he who seeks equity must do equity. In other words, you must come into court with clean hands. You cannot plead your own turpitude, is the English of another Latin law maxim -I wonder why lawyers express their best thoughts in Latin. I have in mind two cases which very well illustrate my point; one occurred a number of years ago and the other, curiously enough, happened within the last two or three months. A man murdered someone whose life was heavily insured in his favour. He was indicted on a charge of murder and convicted. In the death cell it occurred to him that the insurance policy was made payable to himself. Whether he was conscience stricken and wished to give the money to the children of his victim or to pass it on to his own wife and family I know not, but he sued the insurance company for the policy moneys. The insurance company said: We are not trying to evade our obligations, we are simply asking for the ruling of this court-one of the highest in England- whether it is consistent with public policy that we should pay this money to the murderer of the insured victim. In that, as in the other case, the court decided that while the insurance policy was quite valid, the money should not be paid over to the claimant because it was against public policy and would be tantamount to encouraging murder.
Let me give the committee another illustration before I conclude my remarks. Many years ago an act was introduced in the British House of Commons to legalize marriage with a deceased wife's sister. One of the members, Colonel Biggar, was very anxious to marry his deceased wife's sister and took a very prominent part in soliciting support for the bill. The thing became a joke, and I believe for many years it was known among lawyers in the old country as the Biggar Relief Bill I am very much afraid that if we proceed with this bill something similar will happen It will be known as the Bootlegger's Customers' Protection bill, and the name of my hon. friend who introduced it will inevitably be associated with it. I would not like that. I would ask him, looking down the corridors of time to the future, what would be his feelings if someone, say, his little granddaughter, ran in from school one day and in childish innocence asked, "grandad, why do they call you Bootlegger George?" That would be a very sad situation, and I suggest that in view of that aspect, which perhaps has not occurred to my hon. friend, he would perhaps be not unwilling and might even be

Civil Service Act-Returned Soldiers
relieved, if I moved, as I do now, that this committee rise.
Motion negatived.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FORGING OF TRADE MARKS-SALE OF GOODS FALSELY MARKED
speechtext: Notwithstanding the very lengthy and strong condemnation of the proposed measure, I think my hon. friend who has just discussed it (Mr. Neill) has taken a rather narrow view of the whole question. This amendment applies to the forgery or counterfeiting of all trade marks, not in particular the trade marks or labels of liquor, but of all registered or recognized trade marks. It is a matter which has aroused considerable attention throughout the business community of Canada. In so far as the object of the bill is to protect liquor trade marks, I only desire to inform the committee that a great many of the provincial governments have asked for and have approved this legislation.

speechtext: Yes, and the liquor boards of many provinces have also approved it. I have the communications here. The government of British Columbia, through its attorney general, has approved the bill. The liquor board of the province of British Columbia has done likewise.

speechtext: Approved Bill No. 34, the telegram says. The government of the province of Saskatchewan has done likewise. subtopic: FORGING OF TRADE MARKS-SALE OF GOODS FALSELY MARKED
speechtext:
What I would ask my
hon. friend the mover of this bill to do is to allow it to stand in order that we may prepare another amendment to cover the request that we have received from the liquor board of the province of Ontario. While the bill does affect forged liquor labels it also affects all commercial trade marks, apart altogether from intoxicating liquors. It is for the greater protection of trade marks used throughout the Dominion of Canada. I should think the ob- , ject to be attained by the bill a most laudable one. Counterfeiting in trade marks does go on. Personally I conducted a prosecution within three years in western Ontario where the forgery was of the trade mark of Vernor's ginger ale, not intoxicating liquor at all, but a trade mark registered in Detroit and also having registration in Canada, and I remember well the difficulties we had to overcome in regard to the wording of the present section in the Criminal Code of Canada. It is to meet eases of that kind, not especially in regard to intoxicating liquor, but in regard to everything which is the subject of commerce, and involves property rights which we recognize in trade marks and in designs. What I would ask is that the bill be allowed to stand. My present view is that the bill should be adopted, and I think it might well be included with other amendments to the criminal code which the government proposes to introduce at a not very distant date.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERANS RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE TEARS
speechtext:
When this bill was last before the house, I gave notice of an amendment which I proposed to move. It will be found in Hansard of May 19. The object of the amendment was while preserving to Canadian soldiers and to those who had served in the Canadian army or in the army of the British Empire the returned soldiers' preference, to exclude those who served in the armies of the Allies and who had come to Canada after the date of the passing of the act. It was the purpose also to exclude those who served in the armies of the empire other than the Canadian army who may have come to Canada after the passing of the act. That is to say, anyone who was living in Canada prior to the passing of this act and who had served in any of the forces of the empire, either naval or military, still keeps the preference which was accorded to him by the Civil Service Act of 1919. Any who come in the future however will be excluded from that preference. To my mind the suggestion is broad enough; as a matter of fact a great many people have told me that perhaps it is too broad. At any rate however it amply preserves all the rights and privileges of people who at the present time are citizens of Canada and who fought the battles of the empire. On the other hand it enables young Canadians if they so desire to qualify for service in the civil service of Canada and not to be excluded from entering that service by being brought face to face with a preference in favour of persons who by no right or privilege which we can grant them should be allowed a preference over our own people. The amendment which I propose to section 29, subsection 4, of the Civil Service Act, would read as follows:
In all examinations for entrance into the civil service, the persons named on such special list, who are found to possess the necessary qualifications, shall be named in the order of merit on the list of successful candidates above all other candidates, and all other persons who have been on active service overseas, in the military or naval forces of His Majesty during the late war, and were at the time of their enlistment domiciled in Canada, who have left such service with an honourable record, or who have been honourably discharged, or when any persons who have served overseas as aforesaid, have died owing to such service, the widows of such persons, and who, in either case, obtained sufficient marks to pass such examinations, shall, irrespective of the marks they have obtained, be named in the list of successful candidates next after any candidates who

are in the special list mentioned in subsection 2 of this section, and above all other candidates.
The wording of the proposed amendment is substantially the same as that which is already in the Civil Service Act except that it omits reference to members who served in the allied forces.

I have no doubt that the hon.
member (Mr. Power) has made a good presentation of the case he has in mind. I find it somewhat difficult, however, to grasp the full purport of his amendment simply from a reading of it. I do think that those ex-imperials, ex-territorials or men from the old land who were in Canada at the time of the call to the colours should be maintained in any position they already enjoy.

speechtext: No, that is quite right. I want to protect such men. I have no doubt there are. many who joined the allied armies, not British regiments, who may not be entitled to special privileges. It may be that they had just arrived in the country or that they came here under such circumstances and at such a period of time after the war that they were not entitled to special consideration. With my hon. friend I agree that some differentiation might be made in reference to those men. I must say however that as I understand my hon. friend's proposed amendment I am not in a position to support it.
