subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ft-is desirable that the house and the country should have a concrete statement of the terms and objective of the government's tariff policy. I say this because, while the Prime Minister in his own utterances has been very definite with regard to the terms and objective of the government's tariff policy, I find that both in this house and throughout the country many of his colleagues do not take the view that he does with respect to the government's policy. I find also that while in Canada one view is accepted as to the objective which the government has in mind in its policy, in the old country when the same policy is 'being discussed by the representative of this government in England and others, an entirely different objective is put forward as being that of the government. For this reason I deem it desirable, now that the right hon. Prime Minister is in the house, and in the presence of us all, that any difference in view be threshed out between us so that we may know definitely what the views of the ministry are, and whether the objections which we are raising to his views are rightly taken.
I shall endeavour, in giving what I understand to be the Prime Minister's view, to express it in his own words and as a part of his own statements made under circumstances and amid surroundings which I think admit of no misunderstanding. If I take, with regard to Great Britain, what was said1 by himself at the Imperial conference when he was presenting the views of the government to the British government and the governments of the other dominions, I think I shall be doing him full justice, and as regards Canada if I give his view as expressed in this house when the budget was introduced on the 1st of June, in the hearing of all present, and state his tariff policy as it is recorded in Hansard, I hope again I will be adopting a course which will admit of no contradiction.
With respect to the statement at the Imperial conference, it will be found in the summary of proceedings of the conference of 1930, which was presented to parliament by command of His Majesty in November, 1930. That is the British copy; it will be found also in the reprint which I think has been distributed to hon. members of this house. I have in my hand the summary of proceedings presented to the British parliament, and I will quote from page 82, which contains the statement made by the Prime Minister of

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
Canada on October 8. Here the Prime Minister sets forth what he describes as the fiscal policy of Canada. I need not read the whole statement, thought I hope if hon. members have not done so they will take occasion to read it; I will quote just a few paragraphs which seem to me pertinent with regard to the policy in so far as it relates to trade within the empire. At page 82 the Prime Minister is reported as having spoken as follows:
And so I propose that we of the British Empire, in our joint and several interests, do subscribe to the principle of an empire preference, and that we take, without delay, the steps necessary to put it into effective operation. First, we must approve or reject the principle. I put the question definitely to you, and definitely it should be answered.
I need not read the whole of that part, but I come to the next paragraph:
Until this principle is accepted it would be profitless to discuss the application of it in any great detail.
Then a little further on the Prime Minister said:
I shall, however, outline in a broad way our conception of the manner in which it may be employed, and shall qualify the generality of my proposal by indicating the method of its application.
I offer to the Mother Country, and to all other parts of empire, a preference in the Canadian market in exchange for a like preference in theirs, based upon the addition of a 10 per centum increase in the prevailing general tariffs, or upon tariffs yet to be created. In the universal acceptance of this offer, and in like proposals and acceptances by all the other parts of empire, we attain to the ideal of empire preference. I amplify and explain this offer in the following ways:
In the first place, the rate I have mentioned cannot, be uniformly applied. The basis of the proposal is the adequate protection to industries now existent, or yet to be established. Because of this, we must ensure a certain flexibility in the preferential tariff, having regard to the fundamental need for stability in trade conditions; and must take account of such prevailing preferences as are now higher than the general one I suggest.
I think that is sufficient to give to the house in concrete form the essence of my right hon. friend's proposal. May I reverse the order of his presentation and restate in a very few words the proposal in its essential particulars. First, the basis of the proposal is adequate protection to industries now existent or yet to be created. There can be no mistake about that; as far as Canada is concerned, the proposal he makes with regard to trade with the mother country and the other self-governing dominions is based upon adequate protection to industries in existence or yet to be established-that is, of course, industries in Can-
[Mx. Mackenzie King.]
ada. What is meant by "adequate protection" the Prime Minister has indicated at different times, and I will endeavour to show from his references in this house exactly what he means.
That is the basis of the proposal, and what is the offer to Great Britain and the other dominions? After there has been adequate protection for Canadian industries, a preference in the Canadian market is offered in exchange for a like preference in their markets, based upon the addition of a ten per centum increase in prevailing general tariffs or upon tariffs yet to be created. That is to say, there must be tariffs before any preference can be given; there must be tariffs in Great Britain as well as in Canada. No preference can be given unless there are tariffs in the different self-governing parts of the empire which wish to trade with each other. That is why my right hon. friend's proposals were found so difficult not only of acceptance but even of understanding by the people of Great Britain, because they involved a change in the fiscal system of Great Britain, which is not a protectionist but a free trade system. So the next proposal is that as far as Great Britain is concerned, she must change her fiscal policy if she wishes to get any trade with Canada.
How are the preferences to be brought about? The preferences are to be brought about in the language I have just read; not in the way in which we in Canada are accustomed to speak of giving a preference, namely by lowering the tariff as against some other part of the empire in order to give that part a preference in our market. The preference hereafter is to be given by increases in the tariff against other parts of the world, either tariffs which now exist or tariffs yet to be created. That is the next point to understand clearly. A tariff is imposed in Canada, and as a matter of fact before my right hon. friend started out for the Imperial conference he increased the tariff against Great Britain to such an extent as practically to do away with the British preference on many articles. Now that he has raised the tariff, as far as textiles, iron and a few other things are concerned, to a point which virtually prohibits their importation into Canada, he says to the British government, "If you wish to trade with us we will trade with you on the basis of a preference, but the preference can be brought about only by our adding to the tariff which we have already made against the rest of the world, and by your giving us a preference which will put us in a better position, as far as your markets are concerned, than other parts of the world by you

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
also erecting a tariff which will keep others out and let us in". Then, having made clear what he means by the preference principle, and describes as mutual preferences, he says that until this principle is accepted it would be profitless to accept the application of it in detail. Britain and the dominions must approve or reject the principle; they must subscribe to the principle of empire preference,-not the principle of empire preference as it had been understood by all other dominions or by the British government heretofore, but the principle that all parts of the British Empire must have tariffs, in the first instance, affording adequate protection, and then grant their preferences by raising their tariffs still higher as against other countries.
Now, that is the position so far as Britain is concerned. Is it any wonder that my right lion, friend was unable to get anywhere with a proposal of that kind? As I said before, speaking on this subject in the debate ion the address, I do not believe that any government, Liberal, Conservative or Labour, in Great Britain would ever be able to negotiate with Canada a trade agreement on the basis of excluding, at the very outset, British goods through a tariff being raised in Canada to that point which the right hon. gentleman would describe as adequate protection for the industries of this country.
So far as the postponement of the conference is concerned, what boots it one way or the other? If my right hon. friend holds to the ground he has taken, he will get nowhere if he has conferences every year from now to doomsday. He cannot succeed in negotiating with the British government on the basis he has laid down. I say, therefore, that he will either have to change his policy or abandon all idea of effecting inter-imperial trade as between Great Britain and Canada or to any appreciable extent as between Canada and the other dominions.
Let me come now to the position which my right hon. friend has taken, and which the house will find clearly indicated in Hansard of June 1, 1931. at pages 2337-38. Speaking of treaties and the making of agreements with other countries, the Prime Minister says:
That rule is this: Treaties must be mutually advantageous; if they are not they fail, and unless there is a clear appreciation of that fact there cannot be other than failure. This rule was stated very clearly the other day by the president of the United States Steel Corporation. Speaking to the National Foreign Trade Convention on May 28, he said: It is a sound economic principle to sell in markets where the product is needed for consumption and where there is no surplus of the same commodity.
May I point out to the house that all the domestic trade of this country which represents imports is foreign trade to some other country. If hon. gentlemen opposite will only get in their minds that fundamental thought they will realize that this government on the one hand, desires to maintain the economic principle to which Mr. Farrell referred, and on the second hand, to realize to the full that every import brought into this country from abroad represents foreign trade to some other country. Our business is to see that we do not expand the foreign trade of any other country when we ourselves are producing or can produce the goods so imported.
Now, what does that mean? If I were given to the kind of comments which hon. gentlemen opposite so frequently direct to us on this side of the house, I would say that it is extraordinary that my right hon. friend when he is dealing with matters of this sort, should always seek his authorities in the United States. He quoted ex-President Cool-idge with respect to what should be done in regard to public finance, and now he quotes the president of this corporation in the United States. What does Mr. Farrell's statement amount :to? The right hon. gentleman tells us that Mr. Farrell says:
It is a sound economic principle to sell in markets where the product is needed for consumption and where there is no surplus of the same commodity.
I cannot for the life of me detect any principle in that. It is a veiy obvious truism that the best place in which to sell is where someone wants to buy something which he has not got and which he can get only from you. But is that to be the principle on which this country is to carry on trade with other countries? Is it to be the principle that there shall be trade only with some other country that needs something which it cannot itself produce and which we out of a surplus are in a position to sell to it? Are we to trade on that basis and on no other? Are we to understand that we are not to trade in something we are capable of producing and which the other country is also in a position to produce, but only in those things which they cannot produce? That sounds extreme but that is exactly what he means. Listen to what the Prime Minister says in answer to a question of mine. It is in the next paragraph:
Mr. Mackenzie King: How does my right hon. friend propose to expand the foreign trade of Canada under rules of that kind?
Mr. Bennett: It is very simple. Does the right hon. gentleman for a moment mean to say that there are not countries which do not produce the commodities which Canada produces and which they require?
In other words, we are to be limited in our trading to such countries as do not produce the things that Canada produces but which

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
they require. Let me read again what he says immediately following:
Does the right hon. gentleman for a. moment mean to say that there are not countries which do not produce the commodities which Canada produces and which they require? That is what he is trying to say, and I can tell him that the whole theory upon which trade within the British Empire will ultimately be built up is upon the proper appreciation and realization that the requirements of each part can be filled by requisitioning the production of such commodities from other parts of the empire.
In other words, trade within the empire is to consist in obtaining from other parts of the * empire only those things which cannot be manufactured or produced in Canada but which we must have, while our export trade with other parts of the empire is to be restricted to the things they need, the things which they must have, but which they are not producing or manufacturing. That is what the right hon. gentleman's language means, if it means anything at all. Let me repeat the statement he makes:
Our business-	[DOT]
That is to say, our trading policy.
-is to see that we do not expand the foreign trade of any other country when we ourselves are producing or can produce the goods so imported.
If we are producing or can produce the goods so imported-

Evidently
there is no misunderstanding of the Prime Minister's words. If we are producing or can produce the goods so imported, then our tariff is to be so adjusted as to make it impossible to bring in anything from these countries.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To bring in
anything from those countries; I repeat that statement. If I am wrong I wish to be corrected. Let me once more quote the Prime Minister's words:
Every import brought into this country from abroad represents foreign trade to some other country. Our business is to see that we do not expand the foreign trade of any other country-
Or, to put it in the alternative, our business i3 to see that we do not import anything that we ourselves are producing or can produce.
That is the trade policy of the Prime Minister, and he is specific about it. But throughout the country we find exactly what we find in this house to-night-that while the Prime Minister by his silence acquiesces, for he cannot contradict his own statement, some of his own followers take an opposite point

of view, or seek to take it. I fancy that if some of the hon. gentlemen supporting the Prime Minister will stop to consider these policies of his as they affect the parts of the country which they represent, they will be somewhat more hesitant in endorsing those policies and riveting them upon this country for years to come.
The Prime Minister's policy with respect to trade comes down to this: it makes an isolated economic unit out of this dominion. He believes that in Canada we can produce everything we require up to a certain point, and that anything we can produce here we ought to produce, no matter whether it can be obtained elsewhere at greater relative advantage to the consumers of this country. That is to say, the doctrine which my right hon. friend lays down is that of absolute advantage. There must be only absolute advantage. He leaves out of account altogether what is fundamental in all international trade, namely, comparative advantage in exchange-comparative cost of production as between different countries producing things of the same kind. Let me illustrate. Under the Prime Minister's doctrine of absolute advantage, there could be trade between a country like Canada and, say, Cuba. Canada could send wheat, flour and potatoes to Cuba because Cuba needs those things and cannot raise them, and we could get from Cuba oranges or lemons. That is one kind of trading which would be possible under the lines laid down by my right hon. friend. The tariff must be so adjusted as to make that kind of thing possible, but the kind of thing that must be made impossible is for Canada to send to Cuba wheat, flour and potatoes in exchange for refined sugar or cheese, because those things are manufactured or made in Canada or could be manufactured and made here. That is the doctrine of absolute advantage in trade. I would say that anything of that kind restricts trade to the narrowest possible margin.
Let me give another example to illustrate what is meant by comparative advantage in trade. Take a country like Australia. That country can produce wool and manufacture automobiles; Canada can produce wool and can manufacture automobiles; each country can perform the same functions in those particulars. However, Australia has an advantage in the production of wool which Canada does not possess, and Canada has an advantage in the production of automobiles which Australia does not possess. Australia with her climate and her regions available for pasturage and the like can raise sheep and produce wool at a much lesser cost than Canada can, and

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
Canada with her higher development of manufacturing can manufacture motor cars and the like in a way which Australia cannot begin to do. An exchange between Canada and Australia of automobiles for woo! cannot be other than profitable to both. The example which I have given is an example of the only kind of thing which makes possible trading to any great extent. Canada confining her labour and capital relatively to the manufacture of automobiles and Australia confining hers relatively to the raising of sheep and the production of wool, the two countries, exchanging their respective products on the basis of the greater relative advantage which each possesses would be in a better position as respect both wool and automobiles than if each were to devote their capital and labour in like proportion to the export of both wool and automobiles. International trade is carried on on the basis that a given quantity of labour and capital applied to the resources in certain localities will produce better results than an equal amount of capital and labour applied to similar resources in other parts of the world. When you deny that basis of trade, you make trade to any extent impossible.
Under the theory adopted by the Prime Minister I submit that it would be impossible to arrive at any agreement with a sister dominion like New Zealand. Australia, being in a semintropioal zone as compared with Canada in a temperate zone, offers possibilities. For example, oranges which we cannot grow may be set off against lumber and other things which Australia needs but has not. Undoubtedly an agreement could be made with Australia even along the lines suggested by my right hon. friend, but could a similar agreement be made with New Zealand where the climatic conditions are similar to those of Canada? Could an agreement be made with the other self-governing parts of the empire? There is hardly anything which Great Britain i3 manufacturing or producing which we are not capable of manufacturing or producing here, but Great Britain has certain advantages in the production and manufacture of certain things, and we have a very distinct advantage in regard to the production and manufacture of other things. We can offer to exchange those things in which we have a relative advantage for the things in which Great Britain has a relative advantage. That is the basis upon which all trade must be promoted. If we take my right hon. friend's policy as enunciated it means a complete restriction of trade, notwithstanding that the only solution of our industrial and labour problems, especially the problem of unemployment, lies in the extension and development of our trade.
I believe the Prime Minister will agree that I have stated his point of view and his objective wholly correctly. I say that the nearer he can come to making this country a self-sufficing economic unit the nearer he will come to the attainment of his ideal. As he says, if there are some things we are still wanting which we cannot produce, but which have to be brought from other parts of the world, then those things must be brought to Canada from other parts of the empire to the exclusion of other parts of the world. I think that is his point of view. If I may be permitted to put it in a graphic way, he would make of each self-governing part of the British Empire in the matter of its production and manufactures a watertight compartment. If he applied to the other parts of the empire the same doctrines which he has applied to Canada, he would have them produce and manufacture within their own boundaries all that they are capable of producing and manufacturing, and if there are some things which they cannot produce and manufacture then he would throw up tariff walls as against the rest of the world, thereby giving a preference to them as against the other parts of the world, and establish what he terms mutual preferences. Over and above this structure and superstructure created by tariff walls there would be what might exist in the way of the opportunity of freedom of trade with the rest of the world. There is just about as much likelihood of trade flowing into this country under conditions of that kind from nations other than those of the British Empire as there is of the waters of the St. Lawrence flowing over the Laurentian hills. Can a country develop trade with other countries under a policy of that kind?
In connection with the carrying out of his policy my right hon. friend has three powerful weapons at his disposal, and he is using them effectively. I do not think there ever was a man who went ahead with more steam on and with less thought or caution-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not
know what my hon. friends are applauding, but I just said "with less thought or caution." He is going ahead with full steam on but with no thought or caution; it is just a leap in the dark, a running jump in regard to every one of these things. That is the fashion in which my right hon. friend is legislating at the present time.

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
His first instrument is the majority which he possesses in this house and which has permitted him to alter the customs tariff in the most extraordinary manner and which will help him to enact any kind of legislation. As I said this afternoon, no other country has ever altered its tariff in such a manner. He is raising the tariff without rhyme or reason to a height almost beyond imagination. He is making changes in the most reckless fashion, all for the purpose of making of Canada economically a watertight compartment. As he finds that certain changes do not work out he sets to work to make other changes. One of the daily journals compared my right hon. friend to an untried hand in a power house who pulls out one lever after the other, trying them all in turn just to see how they are going to work. When my right hon. friend finds that one will not work, he changes it, as in the case of glass, of potatoes, of gasoline and the like. If it were not the important business of the country that is being tampered with in this fashion, there might be some humour in the situation.
May I give another simile which to my mind is almost as apt. It seems to me that my right hon. friend is like a novice who for the first time tries out a pipe organ. He begins by pulling out the stops at random; he pulls out as many as he can and then one by one puts them back or manipulates them in and out in different order in the hope that by some lucky juxtaposition harmony will ensue. My right hon. friend, as we will know, pulled out one stop, put it back, pulled out another and put it back, and what has been the result?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Good music.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says "good music." I do mot know what sort of an ear he has for music. It may sound like good music to my hon. friend's ear, but to most of the people of this country it sounds like discord indescribable. That is what my right hon. friend has produced thus far.
_ As I have said, he has changed the tariff in the most reckless and ruthless fashion; he has acted in the most reckless and ruthless way just to see what the particular result will be. That is one instrument that he has used-the power of parliament which he possesses in virtue of his majority.
The next instrument to do his will is the power he has obtained from parliament to do as he pleases by order in council, to get away from this House of Commons, to get away from parliament al'togther and do everything just as he wishes by order in council. He has

by the majority at his back been able to get this parliament, to give him the right to legislate by order in council, and then by order in council he proceeds to give tariff rulings tomorrow that will upset some rates in effect to-day. What he seeks is to be free to do just as he pleases under that power of order in council.
The third instrument which the Prime Minister and his colleagues are using is the old fashioned one of propaganda-propaganda used as I have never heard of it being used by the government of any country. The extent to which my right hon. friend has abused the office of government by spreading Tory propaganda at the expense of the treasury is something which I think ought to attract the serious attention of this house and of the country.
Let me say a word or two on this question of propaganda. I see the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) begins to open his eyes and look across at me. He knows pretty well what the propaganda has cost and how the propaganda is being used. Last fall, not very long after having got into office, my hon. friend had a series of advertisements inserted in the press of this country, alt the country's expense.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And they were good ones, too.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That may be my hon. friend's point of view, but I think once 'the public has read them it will not think much of his judgment. These advertisements were inserted in the press generally throughout the country-with a good deal of political discrimination. A return was brought down the other day as to the papers in which these advertisements appeared. There were a number of papers not on the list; for instance, the London Advertiser, which has a pretty good reputation, and the Vancouver Sun, another very good paper, but they did not happen to be thinking the way my hon. friends opposite were thinking, so they were not favoured with advertising. If you look through the return you will find that some of the papers received a very much larger consideration than others, and from the sums paid you will not have much difficulty in ascertaining the political complexion of those thus favoured.
These advertisements have been circulated throughout the country. What is the nature of them? Here is a series of reprints. Each advertisement is in the form of a letter, communication, or epistle, signed by "H. H. Stevens, Minister of Trade and Com-

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
merce." They bear the coat of arms of the dominion and at the top the official title "Department of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa." Now, these advertisements are addressed to all kinds of persons, and each one has a little heading all its own. I ask my hon. friends opposite, can they tell me anything that more resembles a Tory handbook than these advertisements? A Tory handbook- that is all it is, using the public treasury to exploit Tory propaganda on protection.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You did the same
thing.

speechtext:
Never. That, at best, however, is a very poor justification. My hon. friends are getting ashamed already of What they have done. Just listen to this:
To my fellow citizens, in every part of the dominion. To give Canadians work, buy Canadian products!
The next is:
To women, everywhere in Canada. Protect your breadwinner's job!
Then follow others such as:
To Canadian citizens, everywhere in Canada. Do you want more branch factories?
To wage earners, everywhere in Canada.-

Hon. gentlemen opposite are ready to applaud nothing; I have not given even the title. But let them listen to what the wage earners were told:
Don't be penny wise, pound foolish!
And then some others:
To retail merchants, everywhere in Canada. Yours is a grave responsibility!
To Canadian manufacturers, in every line of business. Remember the Golden Rule!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

That is a pretty good injunction to manufacturers.
To government departments, municipal councils, public utility commissions, school boards, etc., everywhere in Canada. Keep tax collections circulating at home!

speechtext:
Undoubtedly there will be plenty of tax collections to be kept circulating.
To heads of families, everywhere in Canada. Cooperation-the keynote to progress.
Not a word about cooperation between nations.
To Christmas shoppers, everywhere in Canada. Choose gifts that give Canadians jobs!
To Canadian citizens, everywhere in Canada. Suppose everybody rocked the boat!
To Canadian consumers, everywhere in Canada. More for your money, and of better quality!
To Canadian citizens, everywhere in Canada. Bring the boys and girls back home!
Will my right hon. friend say that that has not the familiar sound of Tory propaganda? And all this is paid for out of the public treasury, out of the taxes of the people, at a time when they are struggling and having the hardest time they have had for years. Here are some other samples:
To my fellow citizens everywhere in Canada.
This was on December 27-we were getting near the New Year.
Ring out the old, ring in the new!
That sounds like the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
This . set of advertisements is very similar to a series of open letters which was addressed to me by the same firm of Gibbons Limited just before the general election of 1925. Hon. members will recall that at that time a series of open letters was published as advertisements in the press throughout Canada, all in the nature of Tory propaganda. There is something I can respect about that kind of thing. That was Tory propaganda paid for by Tories, and no doubt by those special interests that hoped to benefit from this advertising. But what I have, just been reading is Tory propaganda not paid for 'by the special interests that are going particularly to benefit, but by money taken out of the public treasury, money which represents taxes collected all over the land. I say that is entirely wrong and should not be countenanced for one minute.
My hon. friend says "ring out the old, ring in the new." He would have done much greater justice to the poet whom he is quoting if bearing in mind the view which nations throughout the world must soon be taking of a policy of protection each against all the rest instead of printing only that fine, he had published this verse of Tennyson's, which is a part of the poem he has quoted:
Ring out a slowly dying cause,
And ancient forms of party strife;
Ring in the nobler modes of life,
With sweeter manners, purer laws.
If my hon. friend would publish that sort of thing, something that has truth in it, something that is calculated to help the tone of politics in this country, I imagine the people would forgive him even for using public funds for the purpose. But I say it is an abuse of office and certainly an abuse of power for any administration to take out of the treasury money to circulate Tory propaganda of the type which these advertisements contain.
In this last letter my hon. friend makes reference to a Christmas gift. Having for the

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
purpose of Tory propaganda used the cloak of patriotism in the way in which he has, and having tried several other cloaks in different ways he now turns to the use of ecclesiastical terminology for his appeal on behalf of protection. He makes his appeal in terms that are familiar to those who attend Sunday schools and churches. My hon. friend has the following:
Ring out the old habits of carelessness in buying. For 1931, let this be your creed.
Then he starts in with the creed. After putting it in the form in which he has it, he
says:
If you are willing to embrace this creed, a copy of same artistically executed in colours, and on heavy stock suitable for use as a wall hanger or for framing, is yours for the asking. Just clip and fill in the coupon herewith. Address your envelope as shown on the coupon. Mail it without affixing stamp, for this particular letter will be carried free.
No increase of postage on that particular letter.

speechtext:
I am coming to it. I would have thought that by now my hon. friends would have learned it off by heart. I never before in my life heard hon. gentlemen opposite so anxious to have a creed. It says at the bottom, " Presented by the Honourable Henry H. Stevens, Minister of Trade and Commerce, New Year's, 1931." Presented by him! I noticed in the press around Christmas time that my right

hon. friend and his colleagues were making a great ado over the fact that they had done away with the sending out of Christmas greetings by ministers at the expense of the government, that the ministers had all been told that they must cease this business of having the printing bureau print their Christmas cards and greetings. But this one goes with the compliments of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and it is a New Year's greeting. Let me now read the creed:
My Creed
I believe in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is all new, I suppose, to my hon. friends.
I love her as my home.
Only faint applause that time.
I honour her institutions. I rejoice in the abundance of her resources. I glory in the record of her achievements. I have unbounded confidence in the ability of her people to excel in whatsoever they undertake. I cherish exalted ideals of her destiny as a leader among world nations.
Very, very faint applause. Any reference to other nations does not get much applause from hon. gentlemen opposite:
To her I pledge my loyalty.
My hon. friends are going back on the King, are they?
To the promotion of her best interests I pledge my support. To her products I pledge my patronage. And to the cause of her producers I pledge my devotion.
I understand that this creed has been distributed in the homes and workshops and factories and schools of this country. You can get any quantity of them for nothing. All you have to do is to ask for them. They are being printed by the millions, I imagine, at the public expense. I was surprised, however, the other day to learn that the Minister of Education in one of the provinces, to be specific, the Minister of Education of British Columbia, had given orders that this creed was to be read once a week in the schools of British Columbia. May I say that if we are to make use of the first words in the apostles' creed, in order to substitute throughout our country the worship of Mammon for the worship of God-if we are to do that sort of thing, it would seem that it ought to be begun in the churches and Sunday schools instead of in the public schools of the country. Why have they not given instructions to have this creed placed up in all the Sunday schools of the country? That surely is the place for creeds that are worthy of the name! This

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
is for the purpose of educating the young minds at the public expense. This federal government is going into the business of education with public money, putting this creed into the public schools, and Tory ministers of education are giving orders for it to be read there by the children once a week. I notice that my hon. friend the deputy speaker does not seem to like that. He does not like any interference by the federal government with the schools of the country, and what they are teaching there, but he is supporting the administration which is using the public schools of this country for this purpose.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	If my right hon. friend
would allow me, would he tell me what is wrong with that creed?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is a time and place for everything. As my hon. friend asks me the question, I say that it is not the business of the federal government to be publishing creeds and distributing them throughout the schools and homes and factories of this country. That is not their business.
May I point out to my hon. friend and to others who think like him wherein I see very grave consequences in this kind of thing. If the young mind is to be taught by means of this literature and this creed that they must buy only "made in Canada goods" in order to be good citizens of this country, what is going to come in the way of confusion of mind when, as they grow up and are taught the responsibility of being citizens of the empire, they are given the gospel, not according to Mr. Stevens, who is a member of the present administration, but the gospel according to the Hon. Howard Ferguson, High Commissioner for Canada and representative of this government in London, who preaches a quite different gospel

not "Canada first" but "Empire first"? My right hon. friend has said that the high commissioner's duty in London is to reflect the policy of this administration originated and initiated in Canada; that, further, his duty in London is to reflect the spirit and attitude of mind of the administration with respect to the problems which they have over there. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce has given us the protectionist policy in Canada in terms of "Buy in Canada." What has Mr. Ferguson been saying in London? I have here a statement taken from an address delivered by Mr. Ferguson as high commissioner, speaking at the luncheon of the Canadian chamber of commerce on March 10, 1931. This is what he says:
When I see in England such slogans as-
This, remember, is the Canadian government speaking in London. It is the man who, in England, speaks, as the Prime Minister said, as a member of the administration:
When I see in England such slogans as "Buy British goods made in England by British labour" it seems to me to be forgotten that goods of Canada and other parts of the empire are equally British. Imperial consolidation cannot be effected on the lines of discrimination.
What is a child to do who has been brought up on this creed of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and then finds himself a citizen of the empire as well as a citizen of Canada? The Minister of Trade and Commerce tells him to buy only goods made in Canada by Canadians, and such like, and Mr. Ferguson tells him and all citizens of the Empire that the term " British goods " applies equally to all parts of the empire-in other words are the same in Canada as Canadian goods or rather that "buy British goods" is not right in Britain when in Canada "buy Canadian goods" is all right. The same kind of narrow doctrine that is preached here in Canada by the minister of Trade and Commerce and his protectionist friends Mr. Ferguson objects to when it is preached in England by the protectionists there.
May I quote one line from the opening letter of the Minister of Trade and Com-, merce, in which he urges people to buy Canadian goods to provide work for Canadians. Keep in mind what Mr. Ferguson says to the person who advocates buying English goods: "It seems to be forgotten that goods of Canada and other parts of the empire are equally British." This is but the equivalent in Britain of what Mr. Stevens has said in Canada:
Every time we buy an imported article-
One from England.
-when we might just as easily have found a Canadian article to serve our purpose equally well, we are helping to do some fellow Canadian out of a job, and making the job of some foreign workman just that much more secure. Conversely, every time we purposely give the preference to a Canadian article, we are helping to create employment for Canadian workers, and doing our bit towards making Canada as a whole more prosperous.
No one in Britain, according to an identical doctrine, would be permitted to buy any Canadian goods, Mr. Ferguson nowithstanding. From the beginning to the end of this series of letters there is not a word which suggests that empire products are to be regarded in any way different from other products. At the same time Mr. Ferguson in London admonishes the British people to remember that

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
all empire goods are British goods and ought to be placed on a parity with goods actually made in Great Britain. How are these policies to be reconciled? First of all I should like to ask the Prime Minister-and I hope if he speaks again he will tell us-which of these policies he supports. Does he support the policy of his government as enunciated in Canada by his Minister of Trade and Commerce, or the policy of his government as enunciated by his representative in London?
What, by the way, does the Prime Minister of Canada say about his London representative interfering in the domestic affairs of Great Britain? I should like to know what business the High Commissioner for Canada has to comment on any policy of the British government or any action of the British people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wonder what the Prime Minister would say if to-morrow morning the High Commissioner for Great Britain in Canada criticized the letters issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce for Canada in the same way as Mr. Ferguson has criticized the slogans for which British protectionists are responsible. Not very long ago my right hon. friend had something to say in this house about interfering in the domestic affairs of other countries. At that time an hon. member was discussing the affairs of Poland and the Prime Minister made the following observation:
When you begin to discuss the internal government of a friendly power, you are on very llangerous ground.
I hope we have not reached the time when we do not regard Britain as at least a friendly power.
It is not the duty of this dominion to undertake to advise people how they should govern themselves.
Well, Mr. Ferguson is doing that. He is telling the British people how they should govern themselves in trade matters. That is something which is entirely their own business. Then the Prime Minister goes on to say:
There is an obligation upon us as a member of the League of Nations, and it is a rather serious obligation, not to reflect upon the other members of that league.
Great Britain is a member of the league just as we are, and I say to the Prime Minister that long before this I think he ought to have taken his high commissioner to task for interfering, not only in this particular but in many other particulars as well, in the domestic affairs of Great Britain.
Speaking of the "Buy in Canada" slogan, may I refer to the fact that recently Canada

was visited by a mission representing what is known as the Federation of British Industries, the report of which mission has recently been issued. According to the statement of its members the mission was invited to Canada by the Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. He is the hon. gentleman who issued all these "Buy in Canada" advertisements. He says, "Buy only Canadian goods." Well, for the information of hon. members may I repeat that he is the hon. gentleman who invited representatives of the Federation of British Industries to visit Canada. What do this mission say? In their report they speak first of all of the different meetings they held. In reference to a meeting held in England while the Imperial conference was in session I find in the report the following statement:
Of special importance were the meetings with the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, Prime Minister of Canada, and the Hon. Mr. H. H. Stevens, the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Before leaving, the mission held several conversations with the Hon. Mr. G. H. Ferguson, the High Commissioner for Canada in London, and a letter was addressed to him setting out the objects of the visit.
Owing to the serious illness of Mr. Stevens, the mission did not leave until April 18, 1931.
Everywhere the mission was most cordially and frankly received. The Prime Minister, during a busy session, gave a long and friendly interview. Mr. Stevens was especially helpful, and the government officials placed themseives unreservedly at the service of the mission.
Then the report follows in the form of a memorandum.
" Canada first " is the policy of this government. Now we shall see what this mission which was invited by the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce to come to Canada, has to say concerning the government's policy. This very interesting report is as follows:
The empire has evolved during recent years into a commonwealth of self-governing nations. The aspiration of the citizens of each nation has been towards self-expression and self determination.
The original political bonds have been loosened, and to-day the dominions are only linked to the empire by the authority of and their allegiance to the crown, and their acceptance of the Privy Council as the highest court of appeal. Such freedom is in accordance with the high traditions of British empire development, but the units of the empire tend to look on themselves as separate nations, forgetting that their force as nations and their security depend entirely on the strength of the British empire as a whole.
The dominions as separate entities are not great nations and Great Britain without the empire loses its unique world position.
Now follows the interesting part of the report:

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
Politicians, the public press and public speakers have raised the cries of "Great Britain first," "Canada first," "Australia first," "South Africa first," and have introduced thereby an undesirable atmosphere of rivalry into empire discussions; but inasmuch as empire unity is essential for the continuing welfare of the British races, national policies should follow the larger issue, and the one cry should be "Empire first".
Hon. members will notice that in this report the statement is made that public speakers have raised the cry of "Great Britain first.''
I think my right hon. friend will take exception to the fact that the cry of "Great Britain first" was the first cry of that nature which was raised. My right hon. friend was the first one to raise such a cry, and his cry was "Canada first." Following him somebody else said "Great Britain first." I do not think he ought to be deprived of the first position, and on his behalf I wish to correct the error which has been made in this report.
I would ask hon. members to notice carefully the language of this report-[DOT]" an undesirable atmosphere " in empire discussions. Speaking of undesirable atmospheres, it is interesting to read what the High Commissioner for Canada has had to say. The High Commissioner for Canada has had some statements to make concerning the Imperial conference, and in the light of some of these statements we are beginning to understand why that conference was the failure it turned out to be. Evidently there was design in it. In a speech at the chamber of commerce in London on March 9, to which I referred a minute ago, the high commissioner is reported as follows in an Associated Press despatch:
Hon. Mr. Ferguson referred to the coming Imperial conference at Ottawa.
This statement was reported on March 10. At this time the high commissioner was thinking cf the conference to be held at Ottawa, though he was referring to the recent Conference in London. The despatch continues: It was not expected that the recent Imperial conference would produce more than the development of a certain atmosphere, he said. The problem involved the whole reconstruction of the economic fabric of the empire.
According to the statement of the high commissioner the conference in London was intended only to produce " a certain atmosphere." The report of the mission of the Federation of British Industries states that the atmosphere which was created was an undesirable one. When one recollects the parting words of the Prime Minister as he left Great Britain there can no longer be doubt as to the undesirable nature of the atmosphere. After spending weeks at the
conference, and after one representative at the conference had made the comment that certain proposals which I have referred to to-night were in the nature of humbug, the right hon. the Prime Minister of Canada gave this parting word which certainly is suggestive of the undesirable atmosphere referred to by this British mission. After referring to the conference to be held in Ottawa-which, by the way, may or may not, as we now know, be held many months or years hence-the Prime Minister writing to the British press, said on the eve of his departure from London:
I have said it is with genuine regret I refer to this statement of the Secretary of State for the dominions. But, in justice to my own country and in justice to the great cause of closer economic unity, there is no other course open. For if this statement indicates what is to be the attitude of the United Kingdom at the conference to be held in Ottawa within the next twelve months, then I have little hope that any agreement which Canada may reach with the other overseas dominions will include the United Kingdom. Holding these views, it is but right that I should express them. Time is running against us. Canada, in her own interests and in the interests of the commonwealth, is honestly working for closer economic association. But if her proposal is to be thus contemptuously rejected, Canadians can only accept the rejection and act accordingly by embracing other means at hand of further strengthening their economic position in the world.
That was the farewell word to Great Britain of my right hon. friend, after he had spent his time at the conference, all ostensibly because the proposal which was outlined tonight in the presence of the house was referred to by one member of the British parliament and government as being in the nature of humbug. I think we have all long since come to the conclusion that such was a correct characterization of the proposal.
Now may I go one step further? While we had the visit from the delegation representing the Federation of British industries, one of the members of the delegation gave an address here in Ottawa. Little by little these things unfold what is apparently at the back of the unpleasant atmosphere which has been created, the atmosphere which the high commissioner said the conference was intended to create. Sir James Lithgow addressed the Canadian Club of Ottawa on May 10, and spoke in the presence of the right hon. Prime Minister. Apropos of the Imperial conference, confirming what I have been saying, Sir James Lithgow, according to the Ottawa Citizen of May 11, said:
"You all know that the Imperial conference at London was pretty much of a failure," Sir James continued. "That is the reason we are here-

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
They were here because the conference was a failure. At whose invitation?
-because Mr. Stevens (Canadian Minister of Trade and Commerce), thought the anti-free trade vote in our federation justified British and Canadian industrialists getting closer together-
What for?
-to see what could be done while the political elements are preparing the way for the next
step."
I wonder what the country will think of this kind of arrangement between the antifree trade forces of different parts of the empire. The Minister of Trade and Commerce for Canada goes to England and says to the protectionists there, " Send out a mission to Canada; we will meet your mission and talk with them about trade between the different parts of the empire, while political forces behind the scenes are getting ready for the next step." Apparently the next step was to postpone any further conference until there is a Tory government in office in England. I say to my right hon. friend that this is hardly the way in which a minister in any country should proceed. I say further to the right hon. Prime Minister that if he is interested in the preservation of the British Empire, as I believe he is, he will cease at once, and have his ministers cease, any kind of alliance with protectionist forces in other parts of the world against any government that may be in office in Britain or elsewhere. The 'surest way to break up the British Empire is to begin to have the political forces in different parts of the empire seek to unite against other political forces, particuarlv the forces of special privilege against those who in different parts of the world seek something in the way of freedom. Sir James Lithgow went on to say:
We admit that unless one looks to the success of one's own business, there can be no general
success.

But Sir James followed with these words:
But the best way to look after one's self is to look after one's customers.
That came home pretty direct from England. He goes a step further:
But the public is being led away by slogans, ....
That was said in the presence of the Prime Minister.
"Canada first" attributed to Mr. Bennett, I believe, and "Britain first" attributed to Mr. 
Thomas. (Laughter). They mean the same thing, these slogans, they mean empire trade. (Applause).
Canada first; Britain first; they both mean the same thing. Where is the applause on the other side now? Then Sir James went on to say:
We are full of hope that the Ottawa conference will not repeat our disappointment of the London conference.
Well, it will not disappoint them this year.
The empire spirit may be greatly injured by the turn of a phrase or an undesirable interpretation put upon some phrase. Here is an opportunity then for the "Canada first" policy.
Is it any wonder that there is confusion in the minds of the people of this country and of Great Britain as to what is the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite? Is it a policy of Canada first or is it a policy of empire first? That is the question we would like to have answered.

speechtext: They mean the same thing.

speechtext:
They are not the same thing; they cannot mean the same thing. Here are two policies which are diametrically opposed. If they are the same, why does Mr. Ferguson find fault in Great Britain with a similar expression of policy to that, of "Canada First" in Canada?
May I say this:	In Canada, to serve a
national purpose we have the horse of "Canada first", carefully groomed, cared for, and trotted out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as a member of this government. Then in Great Britain we have the horse "Empire first", groomed, eared for, and trotted out-instead of "old Fred"-by the high commissioner for Canada in Great Britain. The Prime Minister is trying to ride both these horses at the same time. My right hon. friend has told us many times that he is going to perform many things or perish in the attempt. Let me tell him right now that if he tries to ride these two horses at the same time, "Canada first" and "Empire first", he will find that he has two forces which sooner or later will either collide or so completely separate that he ^ will hasten materially that destruction which he has prophesied for himself. I say it is time the people of this country and the people of Great Britain knew what the government opposite is standing for in the matter of trade relations within the empire.
Now, Mr. Speaker, time does not permit me to develop as I should like to develop-

will go on.

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
What is the result, then, of this policy of economic isolation which hon. gentlemen opposite have begun to put into effect? My right hon. friend said it was intended for what purpose? It was intended to blast a way into the markets of the world. Speaking in Vancouver on June 18-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext: You have said that a hundred times.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext:
Yes, and it will be said one hundred times more. Speaking in Vancouver on June 18, my right hon. friend said:
If Mr. Mackenzie King thinks I will not so build up our agricultural and industrial life that its strength will drive our products into the markets of the world, then he is wrong. For that I will do. If he thinks I will not establish new markets for these products, strive with all my heart to retain them, drive our products with all my power into new markets, into old markets, into reluctant markets, he is wrong. For that I will do.
What has he done up to the present time? Instead of gaining markets he has been steadily losing markets. First of all, he has closed the door against Britain, and I am not sure that he has not slammed it shut, when one considers the parting word with which he left Great Britain after having put up to the British government the proposal which he brought forward with regard to the only basis on which trade would be carried on with Canada. In regard to Russia we know he has slammed the door.

speechtext:
And hon. members praise him for so doing. In regard to Cuba I do not know; perhaps he can tell us whether Cuba has been putting up her tariffs against this country recently because of the treatment he has meted out or was about to mete out to that country, among others, by raising the tariff of Canada.
Let us next consider New Zealand. My right hon. friend strove the other day to have it appear that in some particular the government that was in office before the last election was responsible for the present situation between Canada and that dominion. May I say to him that the government which was in office at that time did give six months' notice to terminate the then existing agreement. He will recollect that it was hon. members of his own party, who were then on this side of the house, who moved a resolution on going into committee of supply, to the effect that the extension to New Zealand of the Australian treaty should be abrogated. They spent months spreading propaganda for the
abrogation of that agreement. When notice was given to New Zealand, care was taken to advise that dominion that on the expiry of the six months, so far as the one article which was occasioning all the discussion was concerned, the duty would be fixed at 4 cents per pound, that being the amount which was suggested by the National Dairy Council of Canada as satisfactory to them. The matter was left in that form, so that the government of Canada could continue negotiations with New Zealand without breaking any agreement or treaty, but with the object of effecting a revision. And that arrangement with New Zealand was apparently satisfactory to that extent, for Mr. Forbes, the Prime Minister of New Zealand, passed through Canada on his way to the Imperial conference, coming here before the period of six months had expired, so that some new negotiations might be entered into and a modus vivendi found for carrying on the agreements between the two countries, with the modification I have mentioned pending the consummation of a new agreement or treaty.
Now, what happened? The very day Mr. Forbes came here my right hon. friend slammed the door in his face. On that very day he put up the rate of duty on butter to 8 cents per pound, making impossible any negotiation meanwhile on the basis which the previous Liberal administration had arranged. In case it may be said that I am wrong in this regard, may I read a Canadian Press despatch from New Zealand which apeared in the Montreal Gazette of June 5, dated Wellington, New Zealand, June 4:
The Prime Minister-
That is, Mr. G. W. Forbes.
-said he hoped Canada would agree to send her minister of trade to New Zealand to negotiate a new trade treaty.
He is making a nice approach.
New Zealand had been forced-[DOT]
Note the word.
-forced to show a strong hand-in placing Canadian imports on the general tariff scale- in view of Canada's "complete failure to listen to representations regarding the butter duty," he said. Mr. Forbes added that, on the day he had arrived in Ottawa,-
That was when my right hon. friend was in office as Prime Minister.
*-Canada had taken an unfriendly action by raising the butter duty.
And then follow these words which are in quotation:
"Canada slammed the door in New Zealand's face at the very time when she was anxious to negotiate," the Prime Minister said.
2704	^	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
Could words be more direct than these? The Prime Minister of New Zealand makes the statement to his own parliament that on the day he came to negotiate an agreement, having come here in the expectation of being able to come to an understanding, ''Canada slammed the door in New Zealand's face at the very time when she was anxious to negotiate."
That is the method which my right hon. friend adopts. Here is an indication of where we are getting to. Who is to blame for the present relationship between New Zealand and Canada? Could anything be more emphatic or direct than the words I hiave just quoted?
Come next to Argentina. The other day we had a very interesting talk by the minister without portfolio, the right hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), who acted as government chaperon to the Canadian manufacturers and members of the Canadian chamber of commerce on their trip to the Argentine. He spent a great deal of time there, and he occupied considerable time in the house telling us about the different places visited by the delegation, and indicating the hopes there were for expansion of trade with that country. What has happened in this regard? This government, under the tariff which they propose, have put up the duty on Indian corn and meats from the Argentine. Surely this country, with the equator lying between it and South America, can hold its own in competition as regards corn and meats coming from the Argentine. But the doctrine of my right hon. friend, of absolute advantage, makes it necessary in his eyes to shut out this trade in meats and corn, though this action on the part of the government is going to prejudice the position of many consumers, as will be readily apparent. The right hon. gentleman seems to think, however, that he must shut it out. Apparently he cannot realize that there may be some comparative advantage in taking some corn and meats from the Argentine, and allowing our producers to ship to the Argentine or elsewhere what they can more advantageously produce, instead of devoting their effort to the sole endeavour to satisfy the Canadian market with all in the way of trade from which those countries are now excluded.
That is the position with regard to the Argentine. We have pretty nearly lost the possibility of coming to an agreement with that country. These ruthless and reckless changes, one after the other, might be described at length, but unless hon. members wish to have them now I will reserve them for another occasion.
Not being satisfied with altering the tariff in the way he has done, my right hon. friend 
has gone a step further and presented to the house a bill to create a tariff board. This is interesting. Observe the way in which the right hon. gentleman works. Either a tariff board is of some service or it is not. If it is of any service, matters affecting the tariff ought first to go before that board for consideration. But my right hon. friend had not been in office an hour before he abolished the tariff advisory board, a board that had been in existence four or five years and had rendered splendid service to the country. He abolished that board. Why? Because he wanted to bring in his changes in the tariff without the possibility of any amendment to refer the proposed changes to a tariff board before they should be carried into effect. He now takes care to put through his budget before the new tariff board is created, so that all the changes will become effective without reference to even a body of his own creation. That shows the amount of faith he has in his changes, and his frame of mind as respects the view which the different interests immediately concerned are likely to take of them.
There is one feature of the proposed board to which I hope my right hon. friend will give a little consideration before he advances his bill any further. He proposes to appoint nominees of his own to that board and to give them a tenure of office of ten years. Now, I have no objection to his choosing, as advisers on tariff matters, any body of men he pleases. But he has no right, after he has made of this country a watertight compartment through his tariff legislation, to try hermetically to seal the whole concern by appointing for a period of ten years those who will have the final say in the interpretation of the tariff as it is being applied, and who with respect to the administration of the tariff will be the last court of appeal from any decision. The government proposes to have the board, with these powers, fastened down upon all possible subsequent administrations within this period of ten years. The thing is entirely wrong. I appeal to my right hon. friend to amend his bill when it comes before us so as to make the appointment of members of the board not for ten years but during pleasure. Let him give his appointees any security he likes. He will find a good many declarations of his own, wherein he has made it perfectly clear that no government, particularly on a matter which admits of as much difference of opinion as fiscal questions, has any right to bind its successors.
I know there are those who think that a subsequent government could repeal such legislation. But let me point out, though a change in administration may not 'be distant, that by the time another government comes into

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
office the chances are that the senate will again be in the position it was politically when the late Liberal administration came into office. During the whole time we were in power we were faced in that house with a majority politically opposed. Legislation put through now, will bind subsequent governments as well as the present administration. Lnless his object is simply to help his own favourite special interests, the Prime Minister had better see to it that the change which I urge upon him is immediately made in the legislation he proposes.
I have tried to picture what I conceive to be the thought in my right hon. friend's mind with respect to the reconstruction of Canada and the reconstruction of the empire, as he evidently has it in view under the legislation which he is introducing. May I in a word say to the Prime Minister what I conceive to be the inevitable outcome of his fiscal policies. If my right hon. friend should succeed in what he is seeking to bring about there is no doubt that there would be a considerable change in the social relations of the different classes of this country and a change in the industrial relations which would be very marked as between the different parts of the country. If I take my right hon. friend's own words as being indicative of what he is aiming at, I gather that what he wants to build up in this country, at all costs, is a number of large manufacturing industries. By means of a very high tariff he believes he can accomplish that end.

speechtext: He is doing it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An hon. member says " He is doing it." But the Prime Minister is not thinking equally of the great primary industries. The other evening the Prime Minister read a list of the new factories and industries which had been established. One of his supporters now says ''He is doing it." My right hon. friend did not tell us at that time how many industries had been established in previous years before his tariff policy was inaugurated, nor did he tell us the extent of capital invested in the establishments he mentioned. He did not tell us whether those establishments were in the nature of mere selling agencies, or the like, or how many people they employed. What was more important, he did not tell us how many failures there have been in industry over the same period of time. My right hon. friend stated that since August there has been an influx of new concerns, eighty-seven of which had been already listed. The Canadian National Railways annual report for
1927 contains a list of new industries which had been established along their line, to a total of 456 new manufacturing establishments. The capital expenditure in this regard was $44,211,000, while additions to establishments along the lines were made to the extent of $29,000,000. This was a period of Liberal administration. In 1930 the Canadian National Railways reported 340 new industries, and if the figures compiled by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had been issued they would have probably shown a corresponding number. Four hundred and fifty-six new industries in one year, three hundred and forty in another, and yet my right hon. friend is boasting of the fact that eighty-seven new industries have been established since August, 1930. The following is a list of business failures for the last few months:
