In other words 331 manufacturing industries died in eight months while 87 were born in ten months. To quote the words of my right hon. friend uttered on a previous occasion, "another such achievement and we are undone."
When my right hon. friend gave that list to the house he made it quite clear that what he had in mind was a special privilege to special interests of a special class. At that time I drew his attention to the fact that all of these industries were, with one or two exceptions, being established in two provinces, and he agreed with my statement. They were all manufacturing industries. Did my right hon. friend have any word in that list to represent any service rendered to the agricultural industry in all of its branches, dairying, horticulture, live stock raising, grain raising and so on? Did he have one word of encouragement for the lumber industry? Did he have anything for the fishing industry? Did he say anything of cheer for the mining industry? No, the benefits were all enjoyed by manufacturing industries which are secondary in character. What does that mean? Should my right hon. friend's plan succeed it will mean that we will in Canada be building up an industrial feudalism. That, in a word, will be the effect of his policies, and is, I believe, his objective. There will be an industrial feudalism whereby all the primary industries will be obliged to pay tribute to these secondary

2706	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
manufacturing industries. It will be, as I have already said, building the pyramid of production on its apex instead of on its base.
More than that, beside tributary industries we will have tributary provinces, we will have the provinces other than the central provinces paying tribute. This industrial feudalism will mean, on the one hand, that certain classes of industry will be. paying tribute to another class, and, on the other hand, there will be a geographical feudalism and payment of tribute.
My right hon. friend has made it quite clear that that is what is in his own mind. In this budget he has made provision for what is intended to be a sort of compensation to those parts of Canada which have to pay this tribute. He has given compensation to the maritime provinces in the form of increased subsidies and duties on coal. He has given another form of compensation, as he thinks, to the western provinces in the form of a five cent per bushel subvention on the transportation of grain for the purposes of export. British Columbia and Alberta receive something in the way of compensation for coal shipped abroad, as well as the supposed benefits ^ of a tariff on coal. If the maritime and prairie provinces, and British Columbia are prepared to accept these sops as compensation for the special privileges given to the manufacturing industry of Ontario and Quebec, then I tell them that they are selling their birthright for a mess of pottage. That is what is going to develop, and it will become more and more marked as the years go by. I put this question to the house: Do we want to build up in this country an industrial feudalism of that sort? Do even the people of Ontario and Quebec, assuming that this plan can be realized, want to see great manufacturing industries built up in their provinces to which other parts of Canada, both industrially and geographically, will have to pay tribute? That will mean a great difference in the social relations of the peoples who go to make up our dominion; it will mean a great difference between the east and west of Canada, between the maritime and central provinces and between western Canada and the central provinces. As time goes on we will have more in the way of difference than of unity in this country.
If this compensation which it is proposed to give in the form of coal duties and subsidies towards defraying the cost of transportation of coal and of wheat for export were bo come out of the pockets of the manufacturers who are to benefit by these special privileges, then something might be said for it, but this compensation is to come in part out of the people

of the maritimes, out of the people of the west and the people of British Columbia. There subsidies are only another word for taxes. They are going to have to pay part of the taxes, they will have, along with Ontario and Quebec to help to meet the cost of subsidies. What seems to be such a generous act on the part of my right hon. friend is of quite a different character when it is closely examined.
The treatment which is to be accorded to these special interests is further heightened and emphasized when one considers the taxation features of the budget. What do they disclose? They disclose that the burden of taxation is being placed upon the backs of the people least able to bear additional taxation; those who are to profit most by these special privileges are the ones who to a considerable degree are going to escape taxation. Who will be the wealthiest men in this country under this scheme if they are not already the wealthiest? Will they not be those who will make their fortunes out of these industries that in this way are receiving special privileges? And these largest fortunes of all are to gain from the exemption feature of the income, tax. What there is in the way of loss of revenue from such exemption will have to be made up by taxes raised in another way. Where does my right hon. friend expect to get most of his taxation? He expects to get it out of the sales tax and from the excise tax of one per cent on everything that comes into this country. What does that mean? The sales tax, as we all know, bears most heavily on the great mass of the people, yet the wealthiest people are receiving a partial exemption on their income tax, and that additional burden is placed on the great body of the people through the sales tax and the excise tax of one per cent on everything imported. Talk about the "death knell of protection"! This is the death knell of everything in the shape of freedom of trade.
Not a single thing can be brought into this country now, no matter where it comes from, that will not have to pay a tax of one per cent; not a single thing. That is where again I object to my right hon. friend's method of doing business. No discrimination whatever is shown. At a time when above all times there should have been some discrimination shown, when there is a heavy burden on the people under present conditions, no matter what my right hon. friend may want to do in the course of years, this year he should have been very careful to see that the burden was not being placed on those least able to bear it. Even in good times in a country such as Canada there has been all through the years on the part of

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
past governments a certain regard for burdens imposed by our climatic conditions. No matter what may be said in favour of the tax on anthracite coal, there is a great deal to be said under conditions such as prevail to-day for not having that tax put on the people of Ontario and Quebec next winter. If it were going to bring anthracite coal from the maritimes or from the west to the central provinces, something might be said in favour of the tax, but it will not. I remember at one time during the period of the war that the government of Canada was very glad to have the United States help us out in a critical situation. When we had a severe winter and had not sufficient coal we sent special emissaries down to Washington and asked the Americans to share with us their supply of anthracite coal so that our people would not freeze and our industries would not be closed down.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And they did.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and they did. Suppose we have some industrial troubles in this country or there are such troubles elsewhere and our supply of coal is restricted, and we have difficulty in getting coal, what is going to be the effect of this tax which my right hon friend is putting upon the people, thus making them pay so much more for their coal? The extra price will not consist merely of the tax; there will be an addition to it when the commodity is sold.
Then take the sales tax. Every government in imposing this tax has made some discrimination between the things that the great mass of the people use, and those things which are not so generally used. For example, oranges are a necessary food for little children. We do not produce any in this country. One might describe them as a poor man's luxury they have almost become a poor man's necessity. Why this year of all years put a duty on oranges? And why put a duty on seeds? And why a duty on all periodicals coming into Canada. No discrimination is shown. He pulls out all the stops and then as he gets complaints pushes them back one by one. [DOT]
This building up of a feudal system in which the wealthy capitalist is to be the modern lord is not a desirable thing for this or any country. The other evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred to the fact, speaking of income tax exemptions, that those who are fairly wealthy were going to pay a little bit more than formerly because of the increase of 2 per cent in the tax on corporations. But he did not tell the House that the Prime Minister had stated in 22110-172}
his budget address that if incomes are derived from dividends received from Canadian corporations, the income is exempted up to the amount of $10,000. Now, from what source are the men in Canada that are fairly wealthy, the wealthy industrialists, getting most of their revenue or income today? They are getting it from these very sources that are going to be exempted, dividends from Canadian corporations. The more one examines the budget, the more one discovers there has been real ingenuity shown in taking the burden off the shoulders of the rich and putting it on the backs of the poor.
Just here may I say that I am very much surprised at the Prime Minister-who, I think in most of these matters is very careful-bringing into the debate the name of one who is a civil servant and not in a position to answer for himself. When my right hon. friend was speaking of the information that he had obtained on the income tax, and proposals he was making he introduced the name of Mr. Walters, commissioner of income tax. I submit that the Prime Minister should not have done that. The government must take full responsibility. They alone can answer for their acts. No civil servant is in a position to speak with regard to any public matter that is being discussed in this house. I repeat, the government must take full responsibility and not try to put blame on the shoulders of anyone else.
If time permitted I think I could show wherein this industrial feudalism now being set up is a complete counterpart of the feudalism of the middle ages. The other day I was looking at Hallam's History of Europe in the Middle Ages to recall just what some of the incidents of feudalism were. Here are some of the more important as enumerated by Hallam.
First there was the right of coining money. The modern parallel is the integrated industrial and financial control by which through interlocking directorates of banks, investment houses and industrial corporations, the regulation of credit may be used to serve the interests of manufacturing, and increase the fortunes of those who hold privileged positions of wealth.
Second, there was the right of waging private war. The modern parallel is found in the relentless struggle for monopoly or combination which is characteristic of the present industrial order when operating behind the walls of a high protective tariff.
Third, there was the exemption from all public tributes except the feudal aids. Here we have a parallel in the exemptions granted
2708	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
to those receiving large incomes under the revisions of the income tax rates as proposed in the present budget.
Fourth, there was the right of freedom from legislative control. It would seem that under the present government manufacturers are to be placed under the special protection of the governor in council. Tariff control has been taken largely out of the hands of the legislature and placed in the hands of the executive.
Fifth, there was the right of exclusive exercise of original jurisdiction in their dominions. Here we have as a parallel the character of the proposed tariff board and the wide powers conferred upon it-a veritable fortification of privilege.	_
IHallam also had this to say of the influences that supported feudalism in the
middle ages:__
Nor were motives of interest left alone to operate in securing the feudal connection, the associations founded upon ancient custom and friendly attachment, the impulses of gratitude and honour, the dread of infamy, the sanctions *of religion, were all employed to strengthen these ties, and to render them equally powerful with the relations of nature, and far more so than those of political society.
Could any statement more accurately describe the influences brought to the support of the industrial feudalism of the present day? The house has listened to the appeal to religion in support of the embargo against Russia, but not until the feudal barons had demanded that their home market should be kept inviolate. Public money has been expended in an appeal to patriotism and sentiment in order to preserve the home market for the manufacturing interests of this country by creating a sales resistance to goods from other countries, regardless of the effect of such a policy of trade _ restriction on the primary industries of agriculture, mining, lumbering and fishing. No appeal to religion, prejudice or patriotism has been omitted in the effort to give Canadian manufacturers a position of privilege under the policies of the present administration.
There is one thing further. Feudalism demanded of its people the oath of fealty and homage. A central feature of feudalism in the middle ages was the oath of fealty and homage which the vassels pledged to their lords. Even here the parallel is suggestive; for the Minister of Trade and Commerce has supplied, at public expense, a creed of which the following are the concluding words:
To Canadian products I pledge my patronage. And to the cause of her producers I pledge my devotion.
I wish to conclude, Mr. Speaker, with what I regard as the most important part of what

I have to say. I have reserved to the last what I feel to be the most serious t5mission of the government, the most serious mistake that it has thus far made, though it has made a great many, and that is the complete indifference it has shown towards the problem of unemployment.
My right hon. friend and his party got into office by promising those who were unemployed throughout Canada not merely that they would find work for them, but that they would end all unemployment. I need not go over the list of those promises, though I am very much tempted to give them to my right hon. friend while he is sitting in a position of responsibility. Their whole campaign in some parts of the country was waged on what they would do to end unemployment. They would call a special session, and they would introduce measures to end unemployment. The whole unhappy condition would be over in a short time if not immediately. To-day the conditions are worse than at any time in the history of Canada.
How did my right hon. friend start out to deal with the situation? First of all he took care not to have a Minister of Labour in this House of Commons but to see that he was in the other chamber of this parliament where he would not be subject to questions from day to day by the people's representatives. Where is the Minister of Labour at this hour? Is he in this parliament ? Is he in this city? He is out in the city of Victoria in British Columbia. Why in the city of Victoria while parliament is in session? So that there cannot be any information obtained from that particular source. Was there ever a greater admission on the part of a government of its complete ignorance of a situation existing throughout a country than that disclosed where the Prime Minister has to delegate his Minister of Labour to go to the Pacific coast, and then later to the Atlantic coast, to discover whether people are unemployed in Canada at the present time, and if so, to what extent? I say that that action on the part of the Prime Minister is of itself evidence sufficient to show how little the government begins to appreciate what the situation in Canada is at the present time.
What has the Minister of Labour said, what has the government said, as to the government policy on unemployment? I asked my right hon. friend at the beginning of the session if he would tell this parliament and this country what he meant when he said, "I will end unemployment." He promised to do so, but he has never said one word which gives us the slightest indication of what he

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
had in mind. He has not spoken in reply to the many motions that have been made on going into supply. He has said nothing when the estimates were up for discussion. He made no reference to unemployment in his speech on the budget. He has ignored the subject altogether. We do not know if the government has any policy on unemployment. Its ministers give us contradictory statements. The Minister of Trade and Commerce the other evening said that this was not the time to ask what measures the government was going to introduce, that we would find out at the end of the session. But I find that the Minister of Labour has made a declaration on the subject. What is it? As it appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of June 6 last it is this:
"The federal government's policy on unemployment.' Senator Robertson said yesterday, "will continue to be one of reasonable assistance to the provinces and municipalities to cope with their respective problems."
That is what the Minister of Labour says, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce says: "We will tell you our policy at the end of the session." What is the country to think of that kind of thing? May I say that if the policy of the government is simply to repeat what they did last session, they will not get much thanks from the unemployed or anyone else. What has been the effect to date of their policy? They have spent not all of the $20,000,000, but they have forced numerous municipalities into bankruptcy, according to the statements of the municipalities themselves. They have compelled provinces to spend more in the way of public money than they otherwise would have spent just in order to receive part of the federal dole, but they have not helped beyond a very limited extent in solving at all the problem of unemployment. If what the Minister of Labour says is to be the government's policy, the government had better let us know it in plenty of time. Whatever its policy is, let us at least have an opportunity to discuss it on the floor of this parliament, and let parliament vote the appropriations that are necessary while parliament is still in session. I say to the ministry that they will have no right in relation to unemployment relief to use governor general's warrants this year for any purpose whatever. Last year when there was a general election and an Imperial conference there was a situation, through lack of time, which would have justified the administration in using a governor general's warrant until the moment parliament could be brought together, but if they do not deal with the unemployment situation at this session and are forced to have money
for the purpose of meeting it next winter,, their only course will be again to call a special or regular session of parliament so that we may discuss here in parliament the situation as it is throughout the country.
May I say that one thing that is greatly aggravating labour at the present time is the view which the ministry apparently is taking, that conditions of unemployment do not amount to so very much, after all. My right hon. friend set the example when he was at Regina. He stated when he came back that conditions in the west were not as bad as they were reported to be. He was followed by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryck-man) who also said that the people of the west were beginning to take an interest in protection and that things were not as bad as they were reported to be. The Minister of Labour at Hamilton made a similar statement, and the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have been telling the country that somewhere just around the corner prosperity is waiting. Yet they know well, if they understand anything, that conditions instead of getting better are getting worse daily. Here is something that is truly amazing and something that if I am not mistaken will affect very much the labour people of this country. I quote from the Ottawa Citizen of to-day:
Victoria, B.C., June 15.-Dominion-provincial summer conference on unemployment was not advisable, Senator Gideon Robertson, Minister of Labour, stated before the conference here to-day of mayors and reeves of British Columbia cities and municipalities. It was too early for such a conference, the minister said. Conditions were already changing because of crop improvement and curtailment of immigration had not become effective. . . . Senator-Robertson said Ottawa had felt apprehension' particularly because of reports of drought in prairie provinces. Recent copious rains had changed matters and only in Saskatchewan were crops damaged in places to the extent that only feed would be harvested. West of the great lakes the situation was more acute than in eastern Canada because of the grain situation. Conditions were improving in the last month. Forty grain vessels had left Montreal, indicating betterment.
So it goes on, the government taking the position, in the face of all that has been said in this parliament, in spite of all that people throughout this country know about conditions* that there is no need for calling any conference this summer because conditions are so much improved. May I say that it is this inability of the government to grasp the situation in the country that is exasperating the people to-day-these declarations that there is no great unrest, that there is no great amount of unemployment. Thesa

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
statements are being read by men and women in distressed circumstances and by others who have become despondent by reason of crop failures bringing them to the verge of bankruptcy. The whole situation has been intensified to the point of exasperation by the budget which my right hon. friend has brought down, imposing the very heavy additional burdens of taxation on the people at this time, and distributing the burden in the manner in which it has been distributed.
May I say to the Prime Minister that I believe that there never was anything done by any government which met with such universal resentment as his action and that of his ministers in exempting from the 25 to 50 per cent graduated scale of income tax those who have the largest fortunes in the land. I say I do not care what the number is of those exempted. If there are only very few of them, so much stronger the reason against the action of the government. ^ The fact that it has been done at all indicates the mentality of the government. It indicates their utter inability to grasp the psychology of peoples, which is a first requisite on the part of all who seek to govern. I do not for one moment suggest that in their action my hon. friends have been governed by personal motives. They would not be permitted to sit in this parliament an hour if hon. members generally believed anything of that kind. What however is suggested by their action? It is that in their minds some advantages can be gained by bringing about a condition where we will have in this country a lot of wealthy feudal lords-industrial lords-who will exercise dominion of a social, industrial and political character. That is a significant fact, and I wish to say that I place the responsibility not alone upon the Prime Minister but upon every member of his government for having permitted legislation of that kind to be brought down in the budget now presented to the house. Knowing hon. gentlemen opposite as I do, I cannot understand how among their number there was not one who was strong enough to stand up and say, "In the name of the people of this country I will resign my portfolio before I will submit to this. If one single minister had gone to the Prime Minister, as was his duty when he saw a condition threatening which was bound to arouse in the people throughout the country a state of resentment greater than has ever been known before, and had handed in his resignation, we should not have had legislation of this kind proposed. That hon. gentlemen opposite have at this time permitted
{Mr. Mackenzie King.]
this legislation to be brought down indicates that they do not possess the first requisite of members of a ministry, namely a due appreciation of what a government owes to the people they are governing at such a critical period as the present.
If I may I should like to conclude with one constructive suggestion. The ministry have done nothing to meet the present situation and I should like, if I may be permitted to do so, to make one suggestion which I would ask its members to consider. The Minister of Labour has said that there is no need for any conference at the present time. I say there is need for two conferences. There is need for a conference between the dominion and the provinces to discuss financial arrangements, and to come to some method of delimiting the fields of revenues and expenditures and so arranging matters that taxes in municipalities, provinces and the dominion alike will not be unnecessarily increased at a time such as this. There is need for a second conference namely a conference of employers and employees, representatives of trades unions, representatives of associations of employers, representatives of provinces and manufacturers, of transportation companies, of agricultural organizations, of representative women's organizations, of all those different bodies which represent an informed public opinion. They should immediately all be brought together here in conference to discuss the best means of meeting the present situation and that which is likely to develop through the approaching winter. At a conference of the kind there should be organized an unemployment relief board which would be in charge of the management of the whole unemployment situation.
During the period of the war it was thought advisable to have a purchasing commission to look after the purchase of supplies required for purposes of war. It was thought desirable also to have a fuel board or a fuel controller to look after the supply of fuel. It was thought advisable also to have a food board with several controllers in charge. The British government found it desirable to have a munitions board to see that the supply of munitions was maintained, and in Halifax at the time of the explosion it was found desirable to have a relief commission which had to do with the expenditure of 820,000,000, the same sum as -was voted for unemployment at the special session of parliament last year. I would suggest that the Prime Minister bring together all the representative bodies I have mentioned, that the gathering be non-partisan in character, its members representing whomever they may so long as they

Questions
are in a position to speak for large representative groups of the community. Let the conference itself construct or name a board to handle unemployment relief for this year so far as the federal government's obligation is concerned. Let that board seek to coordinate the work between the provinces, the municipalities, all public bodies and private organizations. Why should not the Red Cross Society and like organizations be utilized in times of peace as well as in times of war to perform useful services in connection with the unemployed and the needy? I am sure its members would welcome the opportunity.
In Canada to-day there are people who are nearing the verge of starvation and many more are greatly distressed in mind because of the position in which they are placed through no fault of their own. I do not refer merely to the casual labourer, or the trade unionist who happens to be out of employment; I do not refer simply to the man or woman who works with his or her hands. I say, that in many of the homes in this country to-day people of all sorts and conditions are wondering if they are going to be able to keep up premiums on their insurance policies, life, accident, sickness, unemployment and the like; whether they will be able to continue to make provision for the education of their children. In the homes of this country to-day numbers of people are wondering whether they shall be able to continue to carry the mortgages that represent practically all of their savings over a period of years. That is the situation as we have it in Canada today ; and the government sits idly by, exempts the multi-millionaires from a portion of their former taxation and allows the poor of the country to suffer. I say, Mr. Speaker, that unless the Prime Minister and his colleagues take some very speedy steps to meet the situation they will find themselves face to face with a condition in this country with which they as a government will be unable to cope. I make my suggestion in all good faith, not as the leader of a party- and the Prime Minister laughs at it; the Prime Minister laughs!
On motion of Mr. Manion the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Bennett the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
